t: A bone sticking up on top of my shoulder: AC joint dislocation and the hook plate
s: A bump on top of the shoulder after a fall may be an acromioclavicular joint dislocation. Treatment choices by grade, the rationale for hook plate surgery, and its pros and cons.
k: shoulder collarbone clavicle acromioclavicular AC joint dislocation separation hook plate
b: Shoulder A bone sticking up on top of my shoulder: AC joint dislocation and the hook plate Hee Seung Nam, MD, Orthopedic Surgeon · October 31, 2026 Some people come in after falling on the shoulder while cycling or exercising and say, “a bone is sticking up on top of my shoulder.” Often the joint where the outer end of the collarbone meets the acromion of the shoulder blade, the acromioclavicular (AC) joint , has been knocked out of place. How far it is out of place decides the treatment Several ligaments hold the collarbone in this joint. Depending on which ligaments are torn and how badly, we usually use the Rockwood classification, from type 1 to type 6. Grade Condition Usual treatment Types 1–2 Ligaments are stretched or partly torn. Little displacement Brace, ice, pain relievers, rehab. Most improve without surgery. Type 3 The ligaments holding the collarbone are completely torn and the end of the collarbone rides up Non-surgical treatment is often tried first; surgery is considered depending on job, sports and symptoms. Types 4–6 The collarbone rides up a lot or is displaced backward or downward Surgery is recommended in most cases. In short, types 1–2 with little displacement almost never need surgery, type 3 is the range where doctors disagree, and from type 4 up the balance tips toward surgery. Both shoulders before surgery. On the right side of the image (the patient's left), the end of the collarbone sits higher than the acromion. If surgery is done, what are the options? There are two main approaches. Hook plate : a metal plate is laid on top of the collarbone and its hook is passed under the acromion to press the collarbone down. It is easy to align while looking directly at the joint, and because it has been used for a long time its results are well known. Suspension fixation (TightRope, “dog bone,” etc.) : holes are drilled in the collarbone and the coracoid process beneath it, and the two are tied together with a strong cord and button-shaped anchors. In many cases the hardware does not need to be removed later. Fixed with a hook plate. The hook at the left end sits under the acromion and presses the collarbone down. How do the results of the two methods differ? A meta-analysis that pooled studies comparing the two methods in acute type 3–5 dislocations that needed surgery found no meaningful difference in shoulder function scores (Constant, UCLA). Pain scores were slightly lower with suspension fixation. The hook plate also has clear weaknesses. Because the hook sits under the acromion, it can catch or hurt when you raise the arm high. Rarely, the bone of the acromion where the hook rests is worn away. For that reason, once bone and ligaments have healed, usually within a few months, a second operation to remove the plate is needed. Suspension fixation, on the other hand, often needs no hardware removal, but drilling through the coracoid is tricky and loosening of the fixation or re-dislocation has been reported, rarely. So is surgery always better? Not necessarily. In a multicenter randomized study in Canada that split acute type 3–5 dislocations between hook plate surgery and non-surgical treatment, the operated side looked better on X-ray but shoulder function at two years was similar , and in the first few months recovery was actually faster in the non-surgical group. Reoperations were more common on the surgical side. So I do not operate on types 1–2, and for type 3 I decide after talking through job, activity, pain and concerns about appearance. When I do operate, I choose the method that gives that patient the most dependable result; I mostly use the hook plate, whose results are well known and which lets me align the joint precisely while looking at it directly. In return, I always tell patients before surgery that a plate removal operation will be needed. In closing Types 1–2 mostly get better without surgery. Type 3 can go either way, surgical or non-surgical, and we decide together based on your life. If surgery is done , functional results are similar with a hook plate or suspension fixation, and each has pros and cons. Whichever method is used, what matters is that it is one the operating surgeon is familiar with and can do well. This article is general medical information. Treatment can differ depending on the degree of dislocation, associated injuries, age and activity level, so please confirm with an examination. References Pan X, Lv RY, Lv MG, Zhang DG. t: Like being kicked from behind: Achilles tendon rupture
s: A case of a man in his 20s who ruptured his right Achilles tendon during exercise: diagnosis with the Thompson test and MRI, why repair surgery is recommended for young active patients and why tension matters, the step-by-step rehabilitation schedule, and why it is easily mistaken for a muscle strain.
k: achilles tendon rupture thompson test repair rehabilitation sports injury
b: Foot & Ankle Like being kicked from behind: Achilles tendon rupture Hee Seung Nam, MD, Orthopedic Surgeon · November 5, 2026 A man in his 20s came in with pain over his right Achilles tendon after an injury during exercise. In his words, it felt as if someone had kicked him just above the heel . Many people describe an Achilles rupture this way. Diagnosis: the Thompson test and MRI With the patient lying face down, squeezing the calf muscle normally makes the ankle point downward (plantar flexion). This is the Thompson test . In this patient, squeezing the calf did not move the ankle, showing that the Achilles tendon had ruptured. An MRI was taken to confirm the location and extent of the rupture. Preoperative MRI. The arrow marks where the Achilles tendon ruptured. Intraoperative photo. Both ends of the ruptured tendon (arrows) are visible. Treatment: rejoining the tendon and balancing the tension For young, active patients, surgical repair that stitches the torn tendon ends together is usually recommended. At surgery it is very important not only to join the tendon but also to match the tension of both ends. If the tension is off, push-off strength can stay weak or walking can become unbalanced even after recovery. For reference, treatment without surgery using a brace and early functional rehabilitation has also been studied, with good results reported. The treatment is chosen considering age, activity level, time since injury and the gap between the tendon ends. Postoperative MRI. The ruptured Achilles tendon (dark band) is reconnected. Recovery and rehabilitation after surgery The postoperative MRI confirmed that the ruptured tendon had reconnected. But reconnection is not the end; the rehabilitation that follows is very important. Right after surgery: the ankle is immobilized pointing downward (plantar flexion). Afterwards: the ankle angle is gradually moved to neutral and then toward the top of the foot (dorsiflexion). After 6 weeks: partial weight bearing and heel-raise exercises begin. After 3 months: light jogging is possible. After about 6 months: a full return to sport is typical. Easy to miss An Achilles rupture is easily mistaken for a simple muscle strain or ankle sprain, because other muscles still allow some walking after it tears. If you cannot stand on your toes, or heard a 'pop' when you were injured, see a doctor right away. If treatment is delayed, the tendon ends retract and it becomes a chronic rupture . Simple repair is then difficult, and a graft using another tendon may be needed. In closing The Achilles tendon is the strongest tendon in the body, but when it ruptures it brings great inconvenience and a long recovery. Prevent it with thorough stretching and keeping warm before exercise, and gentle stretching afterwards. This article is general medical information. Treatment and rehabilitation schedules can differ with the extent of the rupture and the patient's condition, so please confirm through a medical consultation. References Willits K, Amendola A, Bryant D, et al. Operative versus nonoperative treatment of acute Achilles tendon ruptures: a multicenter randomized trial using accelerated functional rehabilitation . J Bone Joint Surg Am . 2010;92(17):2767–2775.

t: The cause of buttock pain hidden in a lumbar MRI: ankylosing spondylitis
s: A 19-year-old with three years of buttock and pelvic pain, diagnosed with ankylosing spondylitis after sacroiliitis was spotted on the coronal view of a lumbar MRI: how inflammatory back pain differs from ordinary back pain, what MRI and HLA-B27 tests mean, and current treatment principles.
k: ankylosing spondylitis sacroiliitis buttock pain pelvic pain back pain HLA-B27 inflammatory back pain
b: Hip & Pelvis The cause of buttock pain hidden in a lumbar MRI: ankylosing spondylitis Hee Seung Nam, MD, Orthopedic Surgeon · October 25, 2025 A 19-year-old man came in with pain in the right buttock and pelvis that had lasted three years. He rated the pain 10 out of 10, and said that on waking his body was so stiff he could not get up right away. Another hospital had treated it as a back problem and taken a lumbar MRI, and he had been told there was nothing seriously wrong with his discs. But the real cause was hiding in that very MRI. The clue in the lumbar MRI Sagittal lumbar MRI. The discs and spinal canal we usually look at show no major problem. Coronal view of the same MRI. Around both sacroiliac joints (arrows) there are signal changes suggesting inflammation. On the sagittal view (from the side) the spine looks nearly normal. But a close look at the coronal view (from the front) shows inflammation in the sacroiliac joints , where the sacrum meets the pelvic bones. A lumbar MRI is usually taken to look at the discs, so the sacroiliac joints at the bottom edge of the image are easy to miss. Confirming it with pelvic X-ray and MRI Pelvic X-ray (arrows: both sacroiliac joints) followed by coronal and axial pelvic MRI. The pelvic X-ray showed whitened, hardened bone around both sacroiliac joints (sclerosis) and small pits in the joint surfaces (erosions), findings that suggest early sacroiliitis. So we took a new pelvic MRI. Coronal pelvic MRI (fat-suppressed). The bone around both sacroiliac joints appears bright. Axial pelvic MRI. Inflammatory signal runs along the sacroiliac joints. This time the bilateral sacroiliitis was even clearer. On examination, the Patrick test, in which the leg is placed in a figure-four position and pressed, caused pain on the right. Strongly suspecting ankylosing spondylitis, we tested for the HLA-B27 gene, and the result was positive . What is ankylosing spondylitis? Ankylosing spondylitis is an immune disease that causes repeated inflammation of the spine and sacroiliac joints. The immune system misfires and attacks the joints and the places where tendons attach to bone. When inflammation recurs for a long time, the vertebrae can fuse with bone and stiffen, called ankylosis , which gives the disease its name. It usually starts between the late teens and the 30s and is more common in men. It is closely linked to the HLA-B27 gene. In a study of 160 Korean patients with ankylosing spondylitis, 96.3% were HLA-B27 positive. On the other hand, about 4–6% of the general population also carry this gene, and most of them never develop the disease. So a positive HLA-B27 alone does not make the diagnosis; symptoms and imaging are considered together. How is it different from ordinary back pain? The pain of ankylosing spondylitis differs from common muscular or disc-related back pain. The Assessment of SpondyloArthritis international Society (ASAS) considers back pain inflammatory back pain when at least four of the five features below are present. Features of inflammatory back pain Common mechanical back pain Starts before age 40 Any age Gradual onset Often starts suddenly after strain Improves with movement Worsens with movement Does not improve with rest Improves with rest Pain at night that eases after getting up and moving Usually less at night Other features can include morning stiffness lasting more than 30 minutes, buttock pain that alternates between sides, knee or heel pain, and uveitis, a red and painful eye. Why is diagnosis often late? Back and buttock pain is common in young people, and early on X-rays often show no change. In a meta-analysis of 64 studies, it took an average of 6.7 years from the start of symptoms to diagnosis. This patient also went three years without knowing the cause. Even before bone changes appear on X-ray, MRI can show inflammation in the bone around the sacroiliac joints (bone marrow edema). If a young person has back or buttock pain lasting more than three months that matches the features above, it is worth checking the sacroiliac joints too. Treatment and management Ankylosing spondylitis is a condition you live with by controlling the inflammation rather than curing it. It is often treated together with rheumatology, and the main principles of the 2022 international (ASAS-EULAR) recommendations are as follows. Exercise and education: regular stretching and exercise are the foundation of treatment. Swimming, walking and exercises that extend the spine are good, with physical therapy if needed. Quitting smoking: smoking is linked to disease progression, so quitting is important. Anti-inflammatory painkillers (NSAIDs): the first-line medicine for pain and stiffness. If they work well and symptoms persist, they may be taken continuously. Biologics: if NSAIDs do not control the disease, injectable drugs such as TNF inhibitors or IL-17 inhibitors are considered. Steroids: long-term systemic steroids are not recommended for spinal symptoms. In closing Back or buttock pain lasting more than three months at a young age, especially pain that is stiff in the morning and eases with movement, can point to ankylosing spondylitis. Even if you have been told your lumbar MRI is normal, the sacroiliac joints may need a separate look. HLA-B27 only helps the diagnosis; a positive result does not mean everyone has the disease. With early diagnosis, and inflammation controlled through exercise and medication, everyday life can be maintained well. This article is general medical information. Diagnosis and treatment can differ with symptoms and test results, so please confirm through a medical consultation. References Sieper J, van der Heijde D, Landewé R, et al. t: Thought to be cellulitis or an ankle sprain, but it was pus inside the bone: Brodie abscess
s: A red, swollen foot or a long-lasting ankle ache may not be a common sprain or cellulitis but a Brodie abscess, a pus pocket inside the bone. Symptoms, imaging, differential diagnosis and treatment, based on two actual cases and a systematic review.
k: bone infection osteomyelitis abscess brodie
b: Fracture & Bone Thought to be cellulitis or an ankle sprain, but it was pus inside the bone: Brodie abscess Hee Seung Nam, MD, Orthopedic Surgeon · September 17, 2026 A patient in her 70s came in with a red, swollen top of the foot that first looked like cellulitis. A patient in his 20s with long-lasting ankle pain looked like a common sprain. Both turned out to have Brodie abscess, a pocket of pus inside the bone . In both, a single X-ray changed the diagnosis. What is a Brodie abscess? A Brodie abscess is subacute osteomyelitis in which pus collects locally inside the bone. It was first described in 1832 by the British surgeon Benjamin Brodie and bears his name. The body cannot fully clear the bacteria and walls them off in hard bone, so a rim of whitened, hardened bone forms around the pocket of pus. This disease is easy to miss because it does not look like an acute infection . A systematic review that pooled 407 reported cases up to 2019 found the following. Item Findings of the systematic review Age and sex Many young patients (median age 17), with men about twice as common as women Time to diagnosis A median of 12 weeks after symptoms began Symptoms Pain in 98%, swelling in 53%. 84% had no fever Blood tests Inflammatory markers were raised in fewer than half Causative organism Staphylococcus aureus was the most common at 67% Treatment Surgery in 94% and prolonged antibiotics in 77% Recurrence 15.6% recurred and needed further treatment With no fever and blood tests near normal, it is easy to write it off as a sprain, growing pains or muscle pain, and the diagnosis is delayed. Case 1. A patient in her 70s who looked like cellulitis A 78-year-old woman came in with a red, swollen left foot. My first impression was cellulitis, an infection of the skin and subcutaneous tissue. She had previously had plate fixation for fractures of the tibia and fibula above the ankle and a knee replacement on the same side. Ankle X-rays before surgery. In the lower left tibia (right side of the image), the bone around the plate is whitened (a sclerotic lesion). The X-ray showed a sclerotic lesion, whitened bone, on the inner side of the tibia, so I added a CT scan. Coronal CT. The inside of the bone is dissolved. Sagittal CT. The pocket of pus has broken through the membrane covering the bone (the periosteum). The CT confirmed inflammation and a pocket of pus inside the bone, with pus that had broken through the periosteum surrounding the bone and spread outside. That is why the skin was red and swollen. Surgery went as follows. I removed the plate on the outer fibula and, through that space, placed antibiotic cement beads mixed with vancomycin inside the tibia. Antibiotic beads release a high concentration of antibiotic at the site of infection for a long time. AP view after surgery. The fibular plate was removed and antibiotic beads were placed inside the tibia. Lateral view after surgery. The plate on the inner tibia was left in place. I did not remove the plate on the inner tibia. Thinking only of treating the infection, it is best to remove all the metal, but removing this plate as well carried a large risk of the weakened tibia collapsing . International consensus defines infection around a plate as a separate entity, fracture-related infection , and the heart of treatment is balancing control of the infection against keeping the bone strong enough to bear load. After this operation I left myself a note: “in chronic osteomyelitis, watch out for fractures in advance.” Afterward the patient complained of pain in the opposite knee, and a lumbar MRI showed pockets of pus around it too, so she was transferred to a tertiary hospital to continue treatment. In an older patient with a history of other surgery, an infection can spread to other sites, so new pain should not be taken lightly. Additional note A typical Brodie abscess occurs in young people with no surgical history. A patient who is older and has a plate, like this one, is unusual, and the picture overlaps with chronic infection at a previous fracture surgery site. It looks the same in that it forms a pocket of pus with a rim inside the bone. Case 2. A patient in his 20s who looked like an ankle sprain A patient in his 20s came in with ankle pain that had gone on for a long time. He had no clear memory of a fall, yet the pain would not settle. AP view of the tibia. There is a round abnormal shadow just above the ankle. Magnified view. Whitened, hardened bone surrounds the area where bone has dissolved (arrow). The X-ray showed an osteolytic lesion, dissolved bone, in the lower tibia, surrounded by a rim of whitened, sclerotic bone. This is the classic appearance of a Brodie abscess. T2-weighted MRI. The inside of the lesion is bright, suggesting it is filled with fluid (pus). Axial CT. The pocket of pus is dissolving the outer bone (cortex) and leaking out (arrow). On T2-weighted MRI the inside of the lesion was bright, suggesting fluid, that is, pus, and on CT the lesion was seen dissolving the outer cortical bone and leaking out. Taking the findings together, I strongly suspected a Brodie abscess. MRI has one more finding that helps tell it apart: on T1-weighted images, the “penumbra sign,” a thin band slightly brighter than its surroundings along the inner wall of the abscess. In a study of 32 patients with subacute osteomyelitis it was seen in 75%, and it is known as a finding that points toward infection rather than tumor. It can be confused with a tumor On imaging, a Brodie abscess can look like some bone tumors, so telling them apart is essential. Condition Usual site and age What helps tell them apart Brodie abscess Ends of long bones (metaphysis), children and young adults A well-defined pocket of pus with a white rim; the MRI penumbra sign Osteoid osteoma Long bones, ages 10–20 Pain that worsens at night and responds well to anti-inflammatory painkillers, a small central nidus and thick sclerosis Chondroblastoma Very end of long bones (epiphysis), teenagers A well-defined lesion at the bone end near the growth plate Ewing sarcoma Shaft side of long bones, children and adolescents Poorly defined spreading bone destruction, onion-skin periosteal reaction, possibly with fever and weight loss For that reason, treatment includes a biopsy to confirm it is not a tumor. If pus is found in the operating room, a culture is sent, and the lesion is cleaned out by curettage along with aggressive antibiotic treatment. In the systematic review as well, most patients received both surgery and antibiotics and results were generally good, but about 15% recurred and needed more treatment. In closing A Brodie abscess often has no fever and normal blood tests, so persistent localized pain may be almost the only signal. If a young person has pain in the lower tibia or ankle lasting more than a few weeks, it is worth checking with a single X-ray . If a site of previous plate surgery turns red and swollen, it may be a bone infection rather than a simple skin infection. It can look like a bone tumor, so treatment includes a biopsy and a culture. This article is general medical information. The same symptom can have many causes, so if pain or swelling lasts, please have it checked. t: Still in pain after the calcium was drawn out with an injection? Calcific tendinitis and arthroscopic calcium removal
s: Most calcific tendinitis of the shoulder improves with non-surgical care and ultrasound-guided needling. What arthroscopic calcium removal adds when it does not, from studies and a real case.
k: shoulder calcium calcific tendinitis calcification arthroscopy needling
b: Shoulder Still in pain after the calcium was drawn out with an injection? Calcific tendinitis and arthroscopic calcium removal Hee Seung Nam, MD, Orthopedic Surgeon · November 1, 2026 “I woke up from sleep with my shoulder feeling like it was being torn off.” This is what patients with calcific tendinitis often say. Calcium builds up inside the shoulder tendon, and when the body dissolves it, inflammation flares and sudden severe pain follows. Let me say first and clearly: most calcific tendinitis gets better without surgery . This article is not saying that “calcium must always be removed by surgery.” If anything, the opposite. What I want to say is that for a few patients who do not get better after treatment in sequence, arthroscopic surgery has a clear role. Treatment has an order Step Treatment Description Step 1 Medication, injection, exercise Anti-inflammatory painkillers, steroid injection at the inflamed site, and shoulder exercises. Many people get better here. Step 2 Ultrasound-guided calcium aspiration Under ultrasound guidance, a needle is used to break up and wash out the calcium. It is one of the most effective treatments that need no surgery. Extracorporeal shock wave therapy is also an option. Step 3 Arthroscopic calcium removal When the treatments above do not work or complications arise, the calcium is removed under direct arthroscopic vision. Ultrasound-guided aspiration is a well-supported treatment. A systematic review pooling 908 patients found that most improved in pain and function, and in a randomized study comparing it with steroid injection alone, the group that also had aspiration did better at one year. But when the same study was followed to five years, shoulder function in the two groups ended up similar. That means calcific tendinitis tends to get better with time on its own. So there is no reason to rush to surgery from the first treatment. So when is arthroscopic surgery needed? The problem is when treatment in sequence still does not work. Pain continues even after one or two aspirations The calcium is hard or widespread and a needle cannot remove enough of it The calcium has burrowed into the bone beneath the tendon. Aspiration results have been reported to be clearly worse in this case. Other problems are present, such as weakness or a stiff shoulder Infection is suspected after the procedure In such cases, arthroscopic calcium removal has shown good results in several studies. As Korean examples, 30 of 35 patients who had arthroscopic surgery for chronic calcific tendinitis had less pain within six months, and in another Korean study the pain score fell from an average of 6.7 to 1.0 out of 10. Arthroscopy lets us see the condition of the tendon directly, and any tendon defect left after removing the calcium can be repaired on the spot. Being able to wash out the joint thoroughly is another advantage. There are drawbacks too. Surgery and anesthesia are needed, and it usually takes three to six months for the pain to settle completely and function to return. Temporary stiffness after surgery is reported in about 10–20%, so rehab is important. In short, there is as yet no evidence that arthroscopic surgery is a better treatment than aspiration “from the start.” But for patients who do not get better with aspiration, arthroscopic surgery is an evidence-based next step. A real case: pain that continued after two aspirations He is a man in his mid-40s. He was diagnosed with calcific tendinitis of the left shoulder and had calcium aspiration at a local clinic, but the pain continued, and after hearing that infection was suspected he had a second aspiration. The pain still did not settle, and he came to the emergency room with a swollen shoulder and weakness lifting the arm. The shoulder was also stiff and hard to move. MRI before surgery. A signal change is seen at the greater tuberosity, where the supraspinatus attaches. Two aspirations had already failed, and infection was even a possibility. Rather than repeat the same procedure a third time, I judged that it was better to look directly with the arthroscope, remove the calcium and wash out the joint thoroughly. As seen through the arthroscope. The area around the tendon is severely congested, and white calcium shows between the fibers. After removing the calcium. The place where the calcium was has been tidied up. As the pictures show, the tissue around the tendon was red and congested from inflammation, and calcium remained inside the tendon. I could remove it while seeing even the parts a needle can hardly reach. In closing Calcific tendinitis mostly gets better without surgery. Medication, injections and ultrasound-guided aspiration come first. If you have aspiration and still do not get better, if the calcium has burrowed into the bone, or if there are other problems such as infection or weakness, arthroscopic calcium removal is a good next step. Recovery after surgery takes several months, so keeping up with rehab steadily is important. This article is general medical information. Treatment can differ depending on the size and location of the calcium, how long the symptoms have lasted and other conditions, so please confirm with an examination. t: An arm hit against a wall after a slip: a long, twisted humeral shaft fracture
s: A case of a long spiral fracture of the left upper arm bone after a slip against a wall: choosing between bracing and surgery, the radial nerve that winds around the humerus, fixation with a long locking plate, and the bone healing after surgery.
k: humeral shaft fracture upper arm spiral radial nerve wrist drop functional brace plate
b: Fracture An arm hit against a wall after a slip: a long, twisted humeral shaft fracture Hee Seung Nam, MD, Orthopedic Surgeon · November 12, 2026 A patient came to the emergency room after slipping and hitting her left arm hard against a wall. She had not lost consciousness, but her left upper arm was very painful and she could not move it. X-ray: a long, twisted break in the upper arm bone Preoperative X-ray. The upper arm bone broke in a long oblique line from the upper part to the middle. Seen from another direction: a spiral fracture, broken by a twisting force. The body, or shaft , of the upper arm bone (humerus) had broken in a long twist: a spiral fracture . This pattern is common when the arm takes a twisting force in a fall. Wait with a brace, or operate? Unlike other long bones, humeral shaft fractures often heal well without surgery. The shoulder and elbow move through a wide range, so a slight bend or shortening of the bone rarely affects function. For this reason, a functional brace that wraps the upper arm while the bone heals has long been used. But bracing has drawbacks too. In a Finnish randomized trial comparing bracing with plate fixation, arm function scores at one year were similar, but a considerable number of braced patients ended up having surgery because the bone did not heal. Wearing a brace for months is also inconvenient. Treatment Pros Cons Functional brace No surgery or anesthesia. Heals well in many cases Brace worn for months. Some do not heal and end up needing surgery Plate fixation Bone aligned and fixed firmly right away. The arm can be moved early Risks of wound problems, infection and nerve injury In this patient the fracture line was long and badly displaced, and she wanted to use her arm soon, so we decided to fix it surgically three days after the injury. Surgery: fixing with a plate while protecting the radial nerve The structure to be most careful about in humeral surgery is the radial nerve . It spirals around the back of the upper arm bone and drives the muscles that straighten the wrist and fingers. If injured, the wrist can droop: wrist drop . About 12% of humeral shaft fractures are reported to come with radial nerve palsy from the injury itself, so the ability to extend the wrist and fingers is always checked before surgery. Fortunately, this patient had no nerve palsy. Through a long incision running from the front of the shoulder down the outer side of the upper arm, the radial nerve was found first at the lower end of the wound and protected throughout. Blood clot and tissue trapped in the fracture were cleared, the spiral fragments were aligned and temporarily held with a wire. A long locking plate was then placed on the outer side of the humerus and fixed with screws into the head above and the shaft below. Intraoperative fluoroscopy confirmed good alignment and appropriate screw lengths. Postoperative X-ray. Fixed with a long locking plate. Postoperative view from the side After surgery: the bone healing Follow-up X-ray. New bone (callus) bridging the break has formed along the fracture. After surgery, the arm was supported comfortably in a sling, and shoulder and elbow exercises began early as the pain eased. Follow-up X-rays showed new bone forming along the fracture as it healed, and she is now doing well. In closing Humeral shaft fractures often heal with a brace, but surgery is considered when displacement is large, when the arm needs to be used soon, or when the bone does not heal. The radial nerve that winds around the upper arm bone can be injured at the time of injury or during surgery, so the ability to extend the wrist and fingers must be checked. If your wrist droops or the back of your hand goes numb after an injury, tell your doctor right away. Whatever the treatment, steady rehabilitation to keep the shoulder and elbow from stiffening is important. This article is general medical information. s: A periprosthetic distal femur fracture above a total knee replacement in a woman in her 70s. What the 3D CT showed, why I chose dual plating over a retrograde nail, reusing the old surgical scar, X-rays and CT before and after surgery, and recovery care.

b: Fracture A thighbone broken above a knee replacement: fixing it with plates on both sides Hee Seung Nam, MD, Orthopedic Surgeon · November 10, 2026 When someone who has had a knee replacement falls, the thighbone just above the implant can break. This is called a periprosthetic fracture , and when it happens above the knee it is a periprosthetic distal femur fracture . This article is about a woman in her mid-70s who had a right total knee replacement some time ago. The thighbone just above the implant broke in a long twisting pattern, and I treated it with dual plating , placing one plate on the outer side and one on the inner side of the thighbone. I will also describe how I weighed a nail inserted from the knee against dual plating before surgery. What is a periprosthetic fracture? A joint replacement is made of metal and plastic that are stiffer than bone. In a fall, stress tends to concentrate just above the border where implant meets bone, and in older people with weaker bone even a minor impact can break it there. It is reported in about 0.3–3.5% of people who have had a knee replacement. It is uncommon but not a minor fracture. Mortality has been reported to be similar to that of hip fractures, so early surgery and getting the patient up and walking early are important. Periprosthetic fractures around a hip replacement were covered in an earlier column . Treatment broadly depends on the state of the implant. If the implant is still firmly fixed: the implant is left in place and only the broken bone is aligned and fixed. If the implant is loose or too little bone is left: a revision is done, replacing the implant with a longer, specialized one. This patient: a long twisting fracture just above the implant She came to the hospital with a fracture of the right thighbone above the knee. She had diabetes and high blood pressure, and blood tests showed anemia, with a hemoglobin level in the 9 g/dL range. Both of these mattered later when choosing the operation. Preoperative front view. The thighbone is broken in a long oblique line just above the implant, with small bone fragments between the fracture lines. Preoperative side view. The fracture line comes down to just above the front edge of the implant. On X-ray it was a spiral fracture , with the bone split along a long twisting line and a few small fragments broken off at the back. There was no sign that the implant had loosened, so I decided to leave the implant in place and fix only the broken bone. Preoperative 3D CT. Rotating it showed how far down the fracture line ran and how the fragments had split. The knee area looks blurred because of the metal implant. The CT confirmed two things. First, the outer end of the fracture line reached the level of the front edge of the implant, so the bone left below the fracture was short , leaving limited room for screws. Second, a long fragment remained attached on the inner side, and putting it back in place would restore the inner column of the thighbone. The dilemma: a nail or two plates? For this kind of fracture with a well-fixed implant, the choice is usually among the following. Method How it fixes Advantages Cautions Lateral locking plate One plate on the outer side of the thigh, held with screws A familiar method that works with any type of knee implant Support comes only from the outer side, so in very low fractures or when the inner side is crushed the inner side can collapse and the leg can bow Retrograde nail A long rod passed through a small incision at the front of the knee, between the implant parts, into the bone Small incision and less bleeding; load is shared along the bone's central axis Depending on the implant design there may be no gap for the rod, and if the bone below the fracture is short there is little room for screws Dual plating One plate on the outer side and one on the inner side Supports both columns, so it holds well even in very low fractures and weak bone Larger exposure, more bleeding and a longer operation Revision arthroplasty Removing the old implant and replacing it with a longer, specialized one Weight bearing is easier right after surgery The biggest operation, with greater cost and complication burden; mainly for a loose implant or too little remaining bone A 2024 meta-analysis comparing plates and nails found no significant difference in the rate of bone failing to heal (plate 9.6%, nail 9.2%) or in reoperation (11.3% and 15.1%). Rather than one always being better, the choice depends on the fracture pattern, the implant type and the patient's condition. At first I leaned toward a nail. A long spiral fracture can be reduced by wrapping cables around it, and inserting a nail through a small incision at the front of the knee reduces bleeding, an important advantage for a patient with anemia. Why I chose dual plating The bone below the fracture was short and weak. With the fracture reaching just above the implant, a single outer plate risked collapse of the inner side. Adding an inner plate grips the short segment of bone near the knee from both sides. It does not depend on the implant type. A nail has to pass through the gap between implant parts, so it cannot be used with some designs. Plates have no such limitation. I could reuse the old surgical scar. Blood reaches the skin at the front of the knee mainly from the inner side. A new incision running parallel beside an old scar can leave the skin between them short of blood. Reopening the old knee replacement scar reached both the fracture and the inner side of the thighbone without adding a new scar alongside it. This mattered all the more because diabetes made wound healing a concern. A long spiral fracture suits cables. Wrapping cables around a long oblique fracture surface holds the two pieces interlocked, so length and rotation can be set before the plates go on. There is published experience with dual plating. A Korean study of 49 patients with distal femur fractures treated with dual plating (29 of them periprosthetic) reported good healing and limb alignment with few complications. A UK study found that dual plating achieved more accurate reduction than a single plate and was a reliable option even for very low periprosthetic fractures. Does dual plating have downsides? The exposure is larger, bleeding increases and the operation takes longer. Stripping the membrane around the bone (periosteum) widely when placing the inner plate can reduce blood flow to the bone, so the rule is to expose only as much as needed. In a patient with anemia, hemoglobin is checked before and after surgery and transfusion is prepared for. The operation Incisions: the front of the knee was opened along the old knee replacement scar and extended upward. A second incision on the outer upper thigh was used to fix the top of the long outer plate; it lies away from the knee, where skin blood supply is less of a concern. Restoring length and alignment: the leg was pulled to restore its length, the twisted fracture surfaces were interlocked, and cables were wrapped around them. Large blood vessels run close to the bone at the back of the inner thigh, so the cable-passing instrument is kept tight against the bone. Outer plate: a long locking plate was placed on the outer side of the thigh, with screws in several directions into the bone beside the implant and fixation up to the middle of the thigh. Inner plate: a second plate on the inner side supported the bone near the knee from the opposite side as well. Check: leg length, rotation, alignment and stability were confirmed with fluoroscopy. Postoperative front view. A long plate on the outer side (left of the image), a second plate on the inner side (right of the image), and cables around the fracture. Postoperative side view. The fracture surfaces are in contact and the implant is in place. The metal staples at the front of the knee close the skin. Postoperative CT. Coronal, sagittal and axial images confirm the position of the outer and inner plates and screws and the reduced fracture surfaces. Care after surgery Moving early: knee bending and thigh-muscle tightening exercises start the day after surgery. Staying in bed brings pneumonia, blood clots and muscle loss quickly. Weight bearing: dual plating is stronger than a single plate, so patients are often allowed to put some weight on the leg with a walker early after surgery. The steps are increased as X-rays show the bone healing. Blood sugar control: diabetes slows wound healing and raises infection risk, so blood sugar needs to be well controlled around surgery. Managing anemia: hemoglobin is checked after surgery, with transfusion or iron supplements if needed. Preventing blood clots: clots form easily in the leg veins after leg surgery, so preventive medication and ankle exercises go together. Treating osteoporosis: if the bone above a knee replacement broke from a minor impact, osteoporosis is likely. Bone density testing and treatment are needed to prevent the next fracture ( osteopenia column ). When to come in right away: swelling, fever or discharge at the wound, a swollen painful calf, or sudden shortness of breath. Key points A thighbone fracture above a knee replacement is uncommon but can be as dangerous as a hip fracture, so it should be treated promptly. Treatment is decided after checking whether the implant is firmly fixed , how much bone is left below the fracture , and the implant type . When the fracture reaches just above the implant and the bone is weak, dual plating that supports both the outer and inner sides can be a good choice. Previous surgical scars also matter when planning the incision for the next operation. Treating osteoporosis and preventing falls are the surest ways to prevent the next fracture. This article is general medical information. Treatment can differ with the fracture pattern, the type and condition of the implant, bone quality and overall health, so please confirm through a medical consultation. t: A 15-year-old's shinbone broken playing volleyball: why I chose a minimally invasive plate over a nail
s: A 15-year-old volleyball player broke both the tibia and fibula landing from a jump. How growth plates, body size, a fracture close to the ankle and the length of available nails led to minimally invasive plate fixation (MIPO), with before-and-after X-rays, a postoperative CT video and the recovery plan.

b: Fracture A 15-year-old's shinbone broken playing volleyball: why I chose a minimally invasive plate over a nail Hee Seung Nam, MD, Orthopedic Surgeon · November 6, 2026 A 15-year-old volleyball player, 180 cm tall, landed from a jump, heard a "snap" and went down holding his left shin. X-rays showed that both the tibia (shinbone) and the fibula (calf bone) had broken in the lower third of the leg, above the ankle. In an earlier column I went through seven cases to outline the treatment options for tibial shaft fractures. This time I follow a single patient and the reasoning behind the choice of treatment. Three things came together here: an adolescent who had almost stopped growing, an adult-sized build, and a fracture close to the ankle. Why shinbone fractures in teenagers are tricky Less natural straightening. In young children, a bone that heals slightly bent largely straightens out with growth. At 15, with growth nearly finished, that ability is weak, and a bend tends to stay. Growth plates may still be open. The tibia has growth plates just below the knee and just above the ankle. In a 15-year-old boy they are closing, so implants must be kept from crossing them. An adult-sized body. Methods that work well for children may not be strong enough for a 180 cm athlete. Watch for compartment syndrome. After a shin fracture, the muscles can swell enough to cut off their own blood supply. He was admitted, splinted and kept elevated, with frequent checks of pain, sensation and toe movement. A CT scan helped plan the operation by showing the direction of the fracture lines and where the small fragments were. A small butterfly-shaped fragment had broken off at the back of the inner side, and the fracture had shifted so the leg bent inward (varus). Four treatment options Method Advantages The catch for this patient Cast No surgery With both bones broken the fracture is unstable and can shift inside the cast, and an above-knee cast is needed for two to three months Flexible (elastic) nails Two thin rods placed while avoiding the growth plates; the standard operation in children In heavier adolescents, healing in a bent position becomes more common Intramedullary nail The standard for adult shin fractures; a thick rod fixes the bone from inside It enters near the growth plate below the knee, and no available nail was long enough for this patient's long tibia Minimally invasive plate (MIPO) A long plate slid under the skin through small incisions; the growth plates can be avoided The fracture is not opened, so a small gap can remain between fragments, and removing the plate later may be considered Why not a nail Flexible nails suit children whose growth plates are wide open. A Finnish study of 56 patients under 16 found that 6 of 26 (23%) treated with flexible nails healed in a bent position, compared with none of 30 treated with rigid intramedullary nails. The authors concluded that flexible nails suit children of 50 kg or less with wide-open growth plates, while more mature adolescents do better with rigid nails. So what about a rigid intramedullary nail ? Two things stood in the way. Growth plate: The nail enters the front of the tibia just below the knee. If that growth plate is still open and gets damaged, the knee can grow into a backward bend. Length: His tibia was long, about 39 cm. The longest tibial nail available to me is 345 mm including the end cap. At that length too little of the nail would sit in the lower fragment to hold it firmly. It is the same limit I met in case 3 of the earlier column. The fracture's location mattered too. Shin fractures close to the ankle more often heal tilted after nailing. In a randomized study of 104 patients with fractures 4 to 11 cm above the ankle joint, 23% of nailed fractures and 8.3% of plated fractures healed with a tilt of 5 degrees or more. A meta-analysis of 8 studies and 455 patients likewise found less malalignment with plates (8.7%) than with nails (24.9%), with no difference in healing or infection. Minimally invasive plate osteosynthesis (MIPO) MIPO is plate surgery without opening the fracture site widely. A cut of a few centimeters is made on the inner side of the ankle, a tunnel is made under the skin, and a long plate is slid upward. The upper screws go in through small stab incisions. Because the muscle and the membrane covering the bone (periosteum) are not stripped from the fracture, the bone heals with its blood supply intact. Plate position: The fracture tended to bend inward, and the small fragment sat at the back of the inner side. So the plate went on the inner side, as a buttress on the side most likely to collapse. Growth plate and joint: The growth plate above the ankle was close to closing. Even so, live X-ray imaging during surgery was used to keep the screws out of the growth plate and the ankle joint. Length and rotation: Since the fracture is not seen directly, leg length and the direction the foot points were matched to the other leg before the screws went in. The fibula was not fixed. Once the tibia is fixed firmly, leg alignment is held, and the fibula carries little body weight and usually heals on its own. His fibula was also narrow, which made placing a rod inside it difficult. In the randomized study above, fixing the fibula as well showed a trend toward slower tibial healing. After surgery The alignment and length of the leg were restored well. As the images show, though, a small gap remains between the fragments. MIPO does not open the fracture to fit each piece together, so a gap like this can remain. A remaining gap does not mean the operation failed. This kind of fixation lets the bone move very slightly so that new bone (callus) fills the space and bridges it. With the blood supply preserved, callus forms well, and 15-year-olds heal bone quickly. In fractures like this, correct alignment, length and rotation matter more than closing every gap. Follow-up X-rays will track the callus filling it in. Aftercare First 1–2 days: Monitoring for compartment syndrome continues after surgery. Pain that painkillers do not control, numb toes or weaker toe movement should be reported right away. Weight bearing: For about the first 6 weeks he uses crutches and only touches down with the toes. Once callus shows on X-ray, weight is increased gradually. Regular X-rays: Healing is checked at set times, such as 6 and 12 weeks. Back to volleyball: With so much jumping and landing, there is no rush. He returns step by step once X-rays show complete healing and leg strength has recovered. Plate removal: The inner shin lies just under the skin, so the plate may be felt or bothersome. Once the bone is solid, removal is usually discussed about 1 to 1.5 years later ( hardware removal column ). Takeaways In adolescents who have nearly finished growing, a shin fracture cannot be counted on to straighten itself as in young children, so alignment needs to be right from the start. Treatment is not decided by age alone: growth plate status, body size, fracture location and even the length of available implants all count. For shin fractures close to the ankle, studies show less malalignment with plates than with nails. Minimally invasive plating may leave a small gap, but with the blood supply preserved, new bone fills it as the fracture heals.

b: Fracture A thighbone broken just above the knee: fixing it with a retrograde nail and cables Hee Seung Nam, MD, Orthopedic Surgeon · November 6, 2026 A break at the lower end of the thighbone (femur), just above the knee joint, is called a distal femur fracture . Young people usually get it in a major accident such as a car crash, but in older people with weaker bones a simple fall from standing can be enough. This article is about a woman in her late 60s who slipped and fell while exercising. Her femur broke in a long, twisting line just above the knee, and we fixed it with a retrograde nail , inserted from the knee end, and cables wrapped around the bone. I will also walk through how we used the preoperative CT to decide which fixation to use. What is a distal femur fracture? The femur is the longest and strongest bone in the body. Its lower end widens to form the top surface of the knee joint. How a fracture here is treated depends largely on whether the fracture line reaches the joint surface. Extra-articular fracture: the joint surface is intact and only the bone above it is broken. The goal is to restore length and alignment and fix the bone securely. Intra-articular fracture: the fracture line runs into the knee joint surface. If the joint surface heals out of place, arthritis can come early, so surgery that lines up the joint surface under direct view is needed. UK data show that distal femur fractures occur in about 10 per 100,000 people a year, and about 85% happen in older people after a fall from standing height. They are less well known than hip fractures but are not minor injuries. In a study of 92 patients over 60, mortality was similar to that after hip fracture, and a 2024 meta-analysis pooling several studies found a one-year mortality of about 26%. Delayed surgery has also been linked to higher mortality, so operating promptly and getting the patient up and walking early matters. This patient: a long twisting fracture above the knee She came to the emergency department after slipping during exercise, with severe pain above the right knee and a visibly deformed leg. Fortunately, sensation, circulation and toe movement in the foot were all normal. Preoperative front view. The lower femur is broken in a long oblique line, and the two fragments overlap, shortening the leg. Preoperative side view. The lower fragment has shifted backward. The X-rays showed a spiral fracture , in which the bone splits along a long line as it twists. The two pieces had slid past each other and overlapped, and the outer shell of the bone (cortex) was thin with sparse bone inside, suggesting osteoporosis. Before choosing an operation, two things had to be checked. First, did the fracture line reach the knee joint surface? Second, was there enough bone below the fracture to hold screws? X-rays alone could not answer either with confidence, so we took a CT scan. Preoperative CT. Several planes and a 3D reconstruction showed how far down the fracture line ran and whether the joint surface was intact. Coronal CT. About 5.3 cm from the outer end of the fracture line to the joint surface. On CT, the joint surface was clean . There was no crack into the knee joint and no fracture splitting the back of the joint surface front to back (a Hoffa fracture). Because the fracture was outside the joint, there was no need to open the joint to line it up. The fracture line, however, came down lower than expected. From the outer end of the fracture line to the joint surface was about 5.3 cm. A nail would need several screws placed in this short segment, so the margin was not generous. Three options Extra-articular distal femur fractures are usually treated with one of the three methods below. None is always better; the choice depends on the fracture pattern and bone quality. Method How it fixes the bone Advantages Cautions Lateral locking plate A plate on the outer side of the thigh, held with screws Works even for very low or intra-articular fractures; many screws can go in different directions Carries load from one side of the bone; in weak bone it can bend or healing can be slow Retrograde nail A long metal rod placed inside the bone through a small incision at the front of the knee, locked with screws at both ends Small incision, less disturbance of the fracture, shares load along the central axis of the bone If the bone below the fracture is short, there is little room for screws, and the nail can wobble in a wide canal Nail + plate A plate added on the outer side after the nail The strongest construct, helpful for early weight bearing in weak bone More operating time, incision, blood loss and cost A UK randomized feasibility study comparing nails and plates (TrAFFix) also concluded that these two methods are the most widely used, but it is still uncertain which is better. Why we chose a nail and cables The joint surface was intact. With no need to open the joint, we could take advantage of a nail placed through a small incision. There was room for screws. We judged that several screws in different directions could be placed in the roughly 5.3 cm below the fracture. A long spiral fracture suits cables. Wrapping cables around a long oblique fracture holds the two pieces firmly together. Reducing the bone with cables before the nail goes in also sets length and rotation. A plate was kept on standby. After placing the nail and screws, we planned to move the knee in several directions under fluoroscopy and add a lateral plate if the lower fragment moved. Adding minimally invasive cables to a retrograde nail has also been reported in Korea. In a study of 15 patients with femur fractures below the narrowest part of the canal (the isthmus) treated this way, every fracture healed, taking an average of 22.7 weeks. Does a plate always have to be added? In older patients with weak bone, a nail or a plate alone may not be strong enough to allow early walking, so combining the two has been described. It is not needed for every patient, though. In this patient, once the cables held the fracture surfaces together, the fixation checked during surgery was strong enough, so no plate was added. The operation Restoring length: traction on the leg brought the two overlapping fragments back to their original length. Reducing with cables: through an incision on the outer thigh, two cables were passed tight against the bone and tightened so the spiral surfaces interlocked. Large blood vessels run close to the bone at the inner back of the thigh, so the cable passer must stay on the bone. Inserting the nail: through a small incision at the front of the knee, the entry point was set precisely, the canal was widened and a long nail was inserted. Its end was buried deeper than the joint cartilage so it would not catch when the knee bends. Locking with screws: three screws in different directions at the knee end and two screws in the upper thigh keep the nail from rotating or backing out. Checking: fluoroscopy confirmed leg length, rotation, knee alignment and stability. Postoperative front view. Two cables wrap the spiral fracture, and the lower end of the nail is locked into the bone near the knee with screws. Postoperative side view. The lower fragment that had shifted backward is back in place, and the end of the nail sits below the joint surface. Postoperative upper thigh. The top of the nail is locked with two screws. The nail was long enough to pass the fracture and reach well up the femur. A short nail concentrates stress at its tip, where a new fracture can occur. Postoperative X-rays showed that leg length and alignment were restored, and the long oblique fracture surfaces were in good contact. Postoperative CT. We checked the position of the nail, cables and screws and how well the fracture surfaces met in several planes. After surgery Moving early: knee bending exercises and thigh muscle tightening start the day after surgery. Long bed rest quickly brings pneumonia, blood clots and muscle loss. Weight bearing: depending on the fixation and bone quality, weight is added gradually with a walker. The steps go up as X-rays show the bone healing. Preventing blood clots: clots in the leg veins are common after leg surgery, so preventive medication is combined with ankle exercises. Treating osteoporosis: breaking a large bone in a simple fall strongly suggests osteoporosis. Bone density testing and treatment must continue to prevent the next fracture ( osteopenia column ). When to come in right away: swelling and fever at the wound, a swollen and painful calf, or sudden shortness of breath. Summary Distal femur fractures commonly occur in older people after a fall and can be as dangerous as hip fractures. Treatment is decided after CT shows whether the joint surface is involved and how much bone remains below the fracture . When the joint surface is intact and there is room for screws, a retrograde nail can be a good choice, and cables help reduce and hold a long spiral fracture. Treating osteoporosis and preventing falls are the surest ways to prevent the next fracture. This article is general medical information. Treatment can differ with the fracture pattern, bone quality and overall health, so please confirm through a medical consultation. References Streubel PN, Ricci WM, Wong A, Gardner MJ. t: A distal humerus fracture into the elbow joint, repaired through an olecranon osteotomy
s: A case of a 43-year-old man whose distal humerus fracture (AO/OTA type C1) extended into the right elbow joint surface after a fall: why CT was needed, the AO/OTA classification, exposing and fixing the joint surface through an olecranon osteotomy with plates, and why rehabilitation to prevent elbow stiffness matters.

b: Fracture A distal humerus fracture into the elbow joint, repaired through an olecranon osteotomy Hee Seung Nam, MD, Orthopedic Surgeon · November 5, 2026 A 43-year-old man came in with right elbow pain after a fall. Front X-ray on arrival. The end of the upper arm bone is broken, and the fracture line extends into the joint. Side X-ray on arrival. The X-ray showed an intra-articular fracture , with the fracture line running into the joint, and it was truly severe. Plain X-rays alone cannot show exactly how many pieces the bone has broken into or which way they have shifted, so we took a CT. 3D CT, side view. 3D CT, front view. The shape of the fracture, including the joint surface, is seen in three dimensions. Diagnosis: distal humerus fracture, AO/OTA type C1 The CT confirmed a distal humerus fracture , a break at the lower end of the upper arm bone, classified as AO/OTA type C1 . A simplified drawing of the AO/OTA classification (red lines: fracture lines). This patient had type C, with the joint surface completely separated from the bone above. In the AO/OTA classification, type C is a fracture that completely involves the joint surface: the bone end that forms the joint has broken away and is no longer connected to the bone above. Within it, C1 is the form in which the fractures of the joint surface and the area just above it (metaphysis) are relatively simple. Unless such a fracture is put back exactly in place, it directly affects elbow movement and function. Surgery: cutting the olecranon to expose the joint surface I put great care into this operation. The joint surface of the distal humerus is hidden behind the olecranon, the bone at the back of the elbow, so it cannot be seen well as it is. We therefore deliberately cut and turned back the olecranon, an olecranon osteotomy , to expose the joint surface. With this view, the bone was put back in place while looking directly at the joint surface (reduction) and fixed with metal plates (fixation). The cut olecranon was reattached with a screw and wire. Postoperative front X-ray. After the joint surface was aligned, plates were applied on the inner and outer sides. Postoperative side X-ray. The cut olecranon was fixed again with a screw and wire. Rehabilitation matters as much as surgery I believe the key to treating elbow fractures is proper reduction and fixation without damaging the joint surface. But surgery is not the end. The elbow is prone to contracture , stiffening that reduces movement, so rehabilitation is as important as the operation. The reason for fixing the bone firmly is, in the end, to allow the elbow to move early. In closing Fractures that reach the elbow joint surface are hard to judge on X-rays alone, so CT is used to check the number and direction of the fragments. A type C fracture that completely breaks the joint surface must be aligned exactly and fixed firmly to preserve elbow function. An olecranon osteotomy is sometimes done to see the hidden joint surface directly. After surgery, steady rehabilitation is needed so that the joint does not stiffen. This article is general medical information. Treatment can differ with the fracture pattern and the patient's condition, so please confirm through a medical consultation. t: A hip neck broken in her 50s: fixing it with an FNS instead of a joint replacement
s: A 52-year-old's femoral neck fracture from a fall, treated with the FNS (Femoral Neck System): the Garden classification, why young patients keep their own bone instead of getting a joint replacement, a 2,038-patient study comparing the FNS with three screws, the actual operation and aftercare.
k: femoral neck fracture hip fracture FNS femoral neck system cannulated screws Garden avascular necrosis
b: Hip & Pelvis A hip neck broken in her 50s: fixing it with an FNS instead of a joint replacement Hee Seung Nam, MD, Orthopedic Surgeon · November 3, 2026 A 52-year-old woman came in with left hip pain after a fall. Tests showed a femoral neck fracture : a break in the neck just below the head of the thigh bone (femur). In the last column I wrote about a periprosthetic fracture in a patient around 90. Even for the same hip, a patient in her 50s calls for a completely different calculation. This is the story of fixing the fracture to save the patient's own bone instead of replacing the joint, and of choosing a device called the FNS . Why femoral neck fractures are tricky The femoral neck is the short neck that joins the round femoral head to the shaft of the thigh bone. The blood vessels to the head run up along this neck, so when the neck breaks, the blood supply to the head can be cut off. Avascular necrosis: a head that loses its blood supply can slowly collapse. Nonunion: the neck takes large body-weight and twisting forces, so it may fail to heal. In a meta-analysis of 1,558 femoral neck fractures in young patients, avascular necrosis occurred in 14.3%, nonunion in 9.3% and reoperation in 18.0% after surgery. These complications were more common in displaced fractures. That is why accurate reduction and solid fixation matter above all. How far has it shifted? The Garden classification Femoral neck fractures are usually graded by the Garden classification , which asks whether the fracture is complete and how far the head has shifted. Stage I Incomplete fracture Head tilted outward and impacted Stage II Complete fracture Not displaced Stage III Complete fracture Partly displaced; head rotated Stage IV Complete fracture Fully displaced and separated A simplified drawing of the Garden classification. Red lines are fractures; thin lines show the direction of the trabeculae inside the bone. Stages I and II are grouped as undisplaced, stages III and IV as displaced. This patient was about stage III. Preoperative coronal CT. A fracture line runs through the neck just below the left femoral head (right side of the image; arrows). The CT showed a fracture line just below the left femoral head, with the head shifted out of place. It can be read as roughly a Garden stage III fracture. Scrolling through the preoperative CT in several planes. We checked the direction of the fracture line and how far it had shifted, then decided how to fix it. Why a joint replacement is not the first choice in your 50s Displaced femoral neck fractures in older patients are often treated with joint replacement. In the early 50s, though, it is a different story. Replacements wear out, so a young patient is more likely to need at least one revision in their lifetime. For young patients the rule is to reduce the fracture precisely and fix it to save their own femoral head , and not to delay surgery. Two options: three screws or an FNS Feature Three-screw fixation FNS (Femoral Neck System) Component Three large screws placed parallel in an inverted triangle A large bolt + anti-rotation screw + small plate working as one unit Principle Each screw holds the head separately The bolt and plate lock together at a fixed angle (angular stability) Pros Long track record, small incisions, lower cost Designed to resist rotation and bending; allows sliding so the fracture surfaces compress and heal Cons May hold less well when the fracture line is close to vertical A newer device with less long-term data; higher cost What does recent research say? An interesting study appeared in 2025 in the Journal of Bone and Joint Surgery (JBJS). Using the hip fracture registry of Kaiser Permanente in the United States, it analyzed 2,038 patients aged 60 and over, comparing the FNS (352 patients) with three-screw fixation (1,686 patients). The rate of reoperation within 2 years was 4.0% for the FNS and 4.8% for screws . The hazard ratio adjusted for several factors was 0.92 (95% confidence interval 0.50–1.71): no statistically significant difference. The result was the same when the comparison was limited to the 72 surgeons who had used both devices. There are caveats. The study included patients aged 60 and over, and this patient was 52. Studies comparing the FNS with screws in young patients alone are mostly small and retrospective. A meta-analysis of them found slightly higher function scores with the FNS and similar neck shortening. My choice: the FNS I used an FNS for this patient. Both methods were evidence-based options, and the difference in reoperation rates in the study was not statistically significant. Still, the number was slightly lower for the FNS (4.0% vs 4.8%). For a young patient whose displaced fracture had to be held firmly in one go, I chose the option that looked even slightly more favorable. The operation After reducing the fracture, we fixed it while checking the position in front and side views on intraoperative fluoroscopy. 1 With the aiming device in place, a guide pin is passed through the center of the femoral neck up to the head. 2 The side view confirms that the pin runs through the middle of the neck. 3 A stepped drill follows the pin to make the path for the bolt. 4 The bolt and small plate are pushed in as one unit. 5 The anti-rotation screw is inserted, and the plate is fixed to the femur with two screws. 6 The final position is checked in the side view. Postoperative X-rays Taken on the way back to the ward after surgery. The bolt and anti-rotation screw reach into the femoral head. A later front view of the pelvis after surgery. The bolt, anti-rotation screw, plate and two screws are visible, and the hip can be compared side by side with the other one. Care after surgery Weight bearing: increased gradually with crutches or a walker, depending on the fracture pattern and fixation. Displaced fractures in young patients often start cautiously. Regular X-rays: avascular necrosis and nonunion can appear 1–2 years after surgery. Even after the bone heals, check-ups continue on schedule in clinic. Symptoms to report right away: if pain in the groin or deep in the buttock returns or worsens, see a doctor without waiting for the next appointment. Bone health: for a woman in her 50s, a fracture from a fall is a good reason to have a bone density test ( osteopenia column ). In closing A femoral neck fracture can cut off blood flow to the femoral head, bringing a risk of avascular necrosis and nonunion. For young patients such as those in their 50s, the rule is to save their own femoral head with precise reduction and solid fixation rather than a joint replacement. In the 2,038-patient study, the FNS and three screws had statistically similar reoperation rates. Accurate reduction and fixation matter more than the device. For 1–2 years after surgery, regular X-rays are taken to check progress. This article is general medical information. Treatment can differ with age, fracture pattern and bone condition, so please confirm through a medical consultation. References Garden RS. Low-angle fixation in fractures of the femoral neck. Femoral Neck System compared with 3 cannulated screws in the treatment of femoral neck fracture in patients aged 60 and older: a multicenter registry-based study . t: A femur broken in a scooter accident: walking again with an intramedullary nail
s: A teenage femoral shaft fracture treated with an intramedullary nail, with real X-rays of the year it took to heal. Covers fracture classification, why nailing is the standard, rehabilitation by stage, and hardware removal.
k: thigh femur femoral shaft fracture intramedullary nail
b: Fracture & Bone A femur broken in a scooter accident: walking again with an intramedullary nail Hee Seung Nam, MD, Orthopedic Surgeon · January 2, 2026 A patient in his late teens came in with severe pain in the left thigh after falling off an electric scooter. The femur is the longest and strongest bone in the body, so a break in its shaft means a very large force was applied. This article follows the course, in real images, from surgery until the bone had fully healed and the metal was removed. Diagnosis: a fracture with a butterfly fragment X-ray before surgery. The shaft of the left femur (right side of the image) is broken and widely displaced. A fracture of the femoral shaft and a detached bone fragment are seen. 3D CT. A butterfly-wing-shaped fragment has broken off between the large upper and lower pieces. The X-ray showed a widely displaced fracture of the femoral shaft, and CT let me examine the shape of the fragments in three dimensions. It was a fracture in which a butterfly-wing-shaped wedge fragment had broken off between the large upper and lower pieces. By the AO/OTA classification widely used for fractures, this is a type B (wedge) fracture . Class Shape Meaning Type A, simple fracture Two bone pieces Subdivided into spiral, oblique and transverse fractures Type B, wedge fracture An additional butterfly-shaped fragment When the wedge fragment is fitted back, the large upper and lower pieces touch each other (this patient) Type C, complex fracture Multiple fragments, or a whole segment Even when fitted together, the large upper and lower pieces do not touch Electric scooters have small wheels, so riders easily fall on small curbs or ice, and a fall at speed produces a high-energy injury close to a motorcycle accident. Fractures with a butterfly fragment or several pieces, as here, are common. Treatment: why an intramedullary nail For femoral shaft fractures in adults and in adolescents who have almost finished growing, surgery is the rule, and the standard treatment is intramedullary nailing , in which a long metal rod is placed in the marrow canal inside the bone. The fracture site is not opened. Because the nail is inserted through small incisions at the hip and knee, the blood clot (hematoma) at the fracture and the surrounding blood supply are preserved, which favors healing. It acts as a pillar inside the bone. The nail shares the body weight with the bone, so walking can begin early. The results have been verified for a long time. In the large 1984 study that established this method, 99.1% of 520 femoral fractures healed and 0.9% became infected. Depending on the entry point, a nail can be inserted through the greater trochanter , the bony prominence on the outer side of the hip, or through the piriformis fossa , the hollow just inside it. In a study comparing the two, healing rates and functional results were similar, but the trochanteric approach had shorter intraoperative fluoroscopy time (average 95 versus 153 seconds) and, in obese patients, shorter operating time. In adolescents with open growth plates, entering through the piriformis fossa risks injuring the blood supply to the femoral head, so I choose the trochanteric entry. For this operation I used a 10 mm diameter, 380 mm long nail inserted through the greater trochanter, and filled the gap between fragments with artificial bone graft. AP view just after surgery. The nail supports the whole femur and is locked with screws above and below. Lateral view just after surgery. The butterfly fragment was not perfectly reduced, but the alignment of the leg was corrected. Why it heals even if the fragment is not perfectly fitted Honestly, looking at the images right after surgery I felt some regret that the butterfly fragment was not an exact anatomical fit. But the heart of femoral shaft fracture surgery is not fitting the fragments 100%, like gluing them. It is correcting length, rotation and alignment , and creating an environment in which the bone can heal on its own. This is called biological fixation . How the bone healed over one year 1 month Callus (new bone) begins to appear around the fracture. 2 months The callus grows denser and bridges the fragments. 4 months The callus hardens and the fracture line fades. 1 year The bone has healed solidly, to the point where the fracture line is almost invisible. In the 1-, 2- and 4-month images, white callus fills in around the fracture, and at one year it had healed so solidly that the fracture line was almost invisible. It is the result of nail fixation that protects the blood supply, combined with a young patient's capacity to recover. Removing the metal after the bone healed AP view after removal. Only the screw holes remain where the nail was. Lateral view after removal. The shape and alignment of the bone are well maintained. I removed the nail after confirming that the bone had healed enough. Whether metal has to be removed, and when, depends on age, site and symptoms. The details are in Do you have to remove the metal plate in your body? . Rehab after surgery: walking again The main goal of nail fixation goes beyond getting the bone to heal: it is to get up and walking as soon as possible . The table below is a general example and is adjusted to the fracture pattern and the rate at which callus forms. Period Goal Main content Just after surgery to 2 weeks Control pain and swelling, prevent joint stiffness Ankle pumps to prevent blood clots, tightening the thigh with the knee straight, starting to bend and straighten the knee 2–6 weeks Walking with crutches Starting at 20–30% of body weight while checking stability on X-ray. In young patients, increase faster if callus fills in quickly 6 weeks to 3 months Off crutches, normal walking If callus is sufficient, full weight bearing, hip and thigh strengthening, stationary bike From 3–6 months Return to sports Start with light jogging, then jumping and cutting sports. Discuss contact sports with your doctor I am often asked, “Do I have to lie in bed until the bone has fully healed?” The answer is no. Appropriate weight bearing stimulates bone cells and in fact helps the bone heal. This patient also rehabilitated actively, and a year later he walks and runs as he did before the accident. In closing A femoral shaft fracture is caused by a large force, and in adults and adolescents intramedullary nailing is the standard treatment. The goal of surgery is less to fit the fragments perfectly than to restore length, rotation and alignment and protect the environment in which the bone heals. The nail lets you walk early, and steady rehab puts the finishing touch on treatment. When riding an electric scooter, always wear protective gear and be careful on ice and curbs. This article is general medical information. Treatment and rehab can differ depending on the fracture pattern, age and associated injuries, so please confirm with an examination.
