t: Fifth metatarsal base fracture: is a cast always necessary?
s: Treatment options for fifth metatarsal base fractures, often diagnosed after an ankle sprain.
k: foot fifth metatarsal jones fracture cast
b: Foot & Ankle · Fracture & Bone Fifth metatarsal base fracture: is a cast always necessary? Hee Seung Nam, MD, Orthopedic Surgeon · December 25, 2025 Sometimes you twist your ankle, go to the hospital, and are given the unfamiliar diagnosis of “fifth metatarsal base fracture.” It is a fairly common injury in which the bony prominence on the outer side of the foot, toward the little toe, is pulled off by a ligament. Once diagnosed, people usually worry about two things: “Do I need surgery?” and “Do I need a cast for a long time?” Surgery is not often needed Acute fractures from a misstep in daily life are mostly treated without surgery. Surgery may be considered, though, when the gap between fragments is wide, when other injuries are present, or in fractures at sites where bone heals poorly, such as an athlete's stress fracture. A cast or a hard-soled shoe Randomized studies comparing a cast with a protective shoe with a firm sole for this fracture have been reported. Pain and bone healing were similar with the two methods, and some results show that return to daily life was somewhat faster with the shoe. The shoe is easier to wash and lighter; the cast gives the reassurance of firm immobilization. What we decide together in clinic Where the fracture is and how far the fragments are displaced Your job, sports and walking plans How much weight to put on the foot during the protection period The protection period is usually given as around a month, but it varies from person to person. Do not stop protection on your own just because the pain lessens; confirm with a follow-up X-ray. This article is general information. Treatment can differ depending on the location and displacement of the fracture, your age and lifestyle, so please confirm with an examination. References Hard-Soled Shoe Versus Short Leg Cast for a Fifth Metatarsal Base Avulsion Fracture: A Multicenter, Noninferiority, Randomized Controlled Trial . J Bone Joint Surg Am . 2021.

t: Hallux valgus: when should you think about surgery?
s: Evaluation of hallux valgus (bunion), shoes and braces, and when to consider surgery, explained from the patient's point of view.
k: big toe bunion hallux valgus
b: Foot & Ankle Hallux valgus: when should you think about surgery? Hee Seung Nam, MD, Orthopedic Surgeon · October 28, 2026 The deformity in which the big toe bends toward the second toe and the bone on the inner side of the foot sticks out is called hallux valgus, or a bunion. Genetic tendency, foot shape and footwear are thought to act together. Not every change in shape needs treatment; pain and difficulty in daily life are the basis for deciding. Assessment in clinic On a standing X-ray I check the angle of the curve and the shape of the bone. Only with weight on the foot can you see the true deformity. I also consider where it hurts, trouble wearing shoes and your usual activity level. What you can try first Switch to shoes with a wide toe box and a low heel Use pads that protect the bump or a spacer between the toes Use anti-inflammatory painkillers when the pain is severe These measures can help reduce pain, but they cannot reverse a bone that has already bent. When surgery is considered We talk about surgery when pain continues even after non-surgical measures have been used well, or when walking in shoes is so difficult that daily life is seriously disrupted. The surgical method differs with the degree of deformity in where and how the bone is cut and realigned, and the surrounding soft tissue is sometimes adjusted as well. The time to put weight on the foot and the recovery period also depend on the method, so it is best to hear the specifics in clinic. What to prepare before the visit One or two pairs of shoes you wear often A note of which movements hurt the most Treatments you have tried so far This article is general information. Treatment can differ depending on the degree of deformity and symptoms, your age and lifestyle, so please confirm with an examination. References American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons. Bunions . t: A bulging lump at the base of the thumb turned out to be a schwannoma growing from a nerve
s: Two schwannoma cases: a large lump on the thumb side of the back of the hand and a small wrist lump. How a lump suspected on MRI to be a giant cell tumor of the tendon sheath turned out to be a schwannoma of the superficial radial nerve, the features and differential diagnosis of schwannoma, nerve-sparing surgery, and recovery.
k: schwannoma nerve sheath tumor hand lump wrist lump nerve tumor Tinel superficial radial nerve giant cell tumor tendon sheath
b: Tumor A bulging lump at the base of the thumb turned out to be a schwannoma growing from a nerve Hee Seung Nam, MD, Orthopedic Surgeon · October 25, 2024 A patient in his early 50s came in with a palpable lump at the base of his right thumb. Even at a glance it looked large and frightening. He said it had appeared after injuring his hand about three months earlier, but it is not clear whether the injury was related. Video showing the first patient's lump (MRI at lower right) and the removed tumor in turn. First patient: the MRI suggested a tendon tumor On MRI the lump seemed attached to a tendon, so we first suspected a giant cell tumor of the tendon sheath . It is the most common tumor of the hand after the ganglion cyst; it is benign but tends to recur after surgery, so I went into the operation quite tense. Before surgery. The back of the hand at the base of the thumb is markedly swollen. Intraoperative photo. The thin strand lifted with forceps is the superficial radial nerve, and the lump had grown beneath it. At surgery the lump turned out not to come from a tendon but to be a schwannoma growing from the superficial radial nerve . The superficial radial nerve is a thin nerve that supplies sensation to the back of the hand on the thumb side. The lump was removed while preserving the nerve, and pathology confirmed a schwannoma. When I told the patient it was not the giant cell tumor of the tendon sheath we had first worried about but a benign schwannoma, he was greatly relieved. The removed tumor. It was about 4 cm long. Cut surface after halving. The yellowish, smooth interior is a typical look for a schwannoma. He has been doing well since surgery. Second patient: a small wrist lump of ten years A 31-year-old woman came in with pain and a lump in her right wrist. The lump had been there for ten years but had recently grown. On examination, tapping the lump produced a tingling, electric feeling. This is called Tinel's sign , an important clue that a lump is related to a nerve. The second patient's wrist MRI. A bright oval lump (arrows) lies just under the skin, slightly above the wrist joint. MRI showed an oval lump a little over 1 cm under the skin just above the wrist joint. It was removed surgically, and pathology again showed a schwannoma. Intraoperative photo. A small yellow lump appeared just under the skin. The removed tumor. Two nodules, each under 1 cm, are joined by a thin strand. She too has been doing well since surgery. What is a schwannoma? A schwannoma is a benign tumor arising from the Schwann cells that wrap nerve fibers. It grows from the outer sheath of the nerve and pushes the nerve bundles aside, so the lump can usually be removed while keeping the nerve. It is common between the ages of 20 and 50 and makes up about 5% of benign soft-tissue tumors. In a UK study of 234 patients, the mean age was 45 and 73% occurred in the arm and hand . In the same study, 98% presented with a lump that hurt when pressed, and 81% had Tinel's sign (tingling when tapped). 31% had pain even at rest, and 20% had reduced sensation. Another feature is that the lump moves side to side but hardly moves along the direction of the nerve. MRI clues and differential diagnosis On MRI a schwannoma appears as an elongated, spindle-shaped mass along the nerve, sometimes with the nerve seen entering and leaving each end. It is bright on T2 images and may show a target pattern with a darker center and brighter rim (target sign). But as with the first patient, when it sits next to a tendon it can be hard to tell apart from other tumors. Lumps of the hand and wrist Feature Ganglion cyst The most common lump: a fluid-filled sac from a joint or tendon sheath Giant cell tumor of the tendon sheath The most common benign tumor after the ganglion; recurrence after surgery reported at around 15% on average Schwannoma Grows by pushing the nerve aside, so it can be removed while saving the nerve; tingles when tapped Neurofibroma Grows intermixed with the nerve fibers, so it is often hard to separate from the nerve Treatment: surgery that saves the nerve If there is pain or tingling, or the lump grows, it is removed surgically. The key is to preserve each nerve bundle under magnification and separate only the lump. Recurrence and malignant change are rare. In the 234-patient study, only 2 tumors recurred after adequate removal, and none became malignant. Temporary tingling may follow surgery. Even with careful handling of the nerve, sensation may be dull or tingly for a while after surgery, and it mostly improves with time. Removing a nerve tumor without knowing it is one is risky. In the same study, 36 patients came back after surgery or biopsy elsewhere because of nerve damage, pain or incomplete removal, and 18 of them needed nerve reconstruction. That is why MRI is used to check the lump's relationship with the nerve before removal. In closing Most lumps in the body are benign. Don't be too frightened at first, and get checked early at a nearby clinic. A lump that tingles when tapped may be a tumor arising from a nerve, so it is best not to squeeze or cut it out casually. A schwannoma can be removed while saving the nerve, and recurrence is rare. If a lump grows quickly, or is larger than 5 cm and deep, a more thorough work-up is needed ( A lump you can feel: lipoma or sarcoma? ). This article is general medical information. Diagnosis and treatment can differ with the location and size of the lump and test results, so please confirm through a medical consultation. References Knight DMA, Birch R, Pringle J. Benign solitary schwannomas: a review of 234 cases . J Bone Joint Surg Br . 2007;89(3):382–387. Di Grazia S, Succi G, Fraggetta F, Perrotta RE. Giant cell tumor of tendon sheath: study of 64 cases and review of literature . G Chir . 2013;34(5-6):149–152. Musculoskeletal Tumor Society. Schwannoma (neurilemoma) . Tumor education.

t: Do you have to remove the metal plate in your body? When is it removed?
s: Do you really need to remove the plates and screws after fracture surgery? A review of 119 hardware removals among 1,040 operations I performed, explaining when and why.
k: plate screw hardware removal implant removal
b: Fracture & Bone Do you have to remove the metal plate in your body? When is it removed? Hee Seung Nam, MD, Orthopedic Surgeon · October 29, 2026 · Hardware removal seen through 1,040 operations There is a question that people who have had fracture surgery ask most often in the clinic: "Doctor, when does this metal come out? Do I have to remove it?" The answer is "it depends on the person and the site." Saying only that would leave you at a loss, so this time I looked directly at my own surgical records. Of the 1,040 operations I performed at three hospitals from March 2023 to October 2026, the operations the surgical record classified as hardware removal numbered 119 (about 11%) . That is about one in ten, a fairly common operation in orthopedics. Of these, I excluded 16 that were not operations to remove metal from the body, such as removing foreign bodies, calcium or loose bodies in a joint, and looked closely at the remaining 103 below. Where was metal removed most often? Number of hardware removals by site (March 2023–October 2026, 103 operations) The most common sites were the wrist and hand (25) and the ankle and foot (24) . Both are where bones most often break in a fall, and the plate sits right under the skin, so it is easy to feel and to cause discomfort. Next came the clavicle (10) , the kneecap (9) and the plate from high tibial osteotomy, HTO (9) . An HTO plate is not for a fracture; it holds the bone after it has been cut to straighten a bowlegged knee. It is often removed once the bone has healed, because it tends to catch under the skin on the inner side of the knee and would have to come out anyway if a knee replacement is done later. By contrast, there were only 2 removals from the femur . I explain why below. Do you have to remove it? If it causes no trouble, most of the time it does not need to come out. Orthopedic metal used today rarely causes problems even after a long time in the body. Removing metal is a real operation too, so anesthesia, a wound and, rarely, risks such as infection, nerve injury and refracture come with it. But in these cases I recommend removal or actively consider it. When the metal can be felt or hurts : where there is little flesh, such as the outer ankle bone, collarbone, kneecap and tip of the elbow, the metal easily rubs against shoes or bag straps. When infection develops : once bacteria settle on the metal surface, removing the metal is often needed to cure it. When screws loosen or the metal breaks When the metal interferes with joint movement or tendons When another operation is planned : an osteotomy plate is the typical example. When a young, active person wants it : we decide after talking it through thoroughly. On the other hand, there are also cases where it is better not to remove it . A large rod placed for a fracture around the hip is a major operation to take out, and there is a risk of breaking again through the old site, so especially in older patients it is usually left in. That is why there are only two femur removals in my records. In places where a nerve runs right next to the metal, such as the humerus, I also weigh benefits and risks more carefully. When is it removed? There is one principle: after the bone has healed completely and firmly . Only once the bone has rebuilt itself to the point where the fracture line cannot be seen on X-ray can it take over the work the metal was doing. I selected 28 patients whose records include both the fracture surgery and the hardware removal for the same person, and calculated the time between the two operations. Time from fracture surgery to hardware removal (28 patients, median about 6.7 months) The median was about 6.7 months . Half of the patients had the metal removed between about 6 and 11 months . 25 of the 28 patients (89%) fall between 3 and 18 months. By site, there were small differences: the shoulder and upper arm (hook plates, etc.) about 5 months, the clavicle 6 months, the ankle and foot about 7 months, the wrist about 9 months and the elbow about a year. But split by site there are only 3 to 8 patients each, so please treat these as rough tendencies. Also, this calculation can use only records from March 2023 onward, so it does not include people whose fracture surgery was before that or who have not yet had the metal removed. For that reason the true intervals may be longer than shown. Only 1 of the 28 had the metal removed within 3 months. Removal this early happens when discomfort is severe or for a special reason such as reoperation. It does not mean "the sooner the better." What is the removal operation like? It is much lighter than the first operation. Based on my records, it looks like this. (Operating time and hospital stay are from 31 operations in 2026 for which records remain; anesthesia and age are from the 72 with records.) Operating time : median 25 minutes, half between 20 and 40 minutes Anesthesia : mostly regional anesthesia that numbs only the lower body or the arm; general anesthesia in 1 of 72 Hospital stay : median 3 days (counted from admission date to discharge date); some went home after a single day Patient age : median 60 years, with 75% in their 50s to 70s Cautions after removal Right after metal is removed, small holes remain in the bone where each screw was. Until those holes fill back in with bone, that area is relatively weak. For that reason I usually tell people to avoid falls and activities with heavy impact for about 6 weeks to 3 months . How long the holes take to fill depends on the site and age, so talk with your doctor about when to return to sports. Rarely, bone comes away with the metal. I once struggled when bone loss turned out to be greater than expected while removing a screw from a small wrist bone (the scaphoid). That is why the principle "if it does not bother you, do not remove it" matters. Frequently asked questions Can I have an MRI with metal in my body? Most orthopedic metal (titanium, medical stainless steel) is MRI-safe. The image around the metal may be slightly blurred. Be sure to tell the staff before the scan that you have metal in your body. Will it set off airport security? Depending on the size and type of the metal, it may or may not. Even if it does, explaining that it is from surgery usually ends with an extra check. Won't it rust or harm the body if I just leave it? Medical metal is made so that it does not rust in the body. If it causes no trouble, most people can keep it for life with no problem. In closing If it causes no trouble , it mostly does not need to come out. If it is removed, it is after the bone has fully healed , usually between 6 months and a year in my patients. For a few weeks to a few months after removal , do not put stress on the bone. Even the same metal has a different right answer depending on site, age and lifestyle. It is best to decide while looking at the X-ray together with the doctor who operated on you. If you have questions, please write to doctornhs@naver.com . The statistics in this article were compiled, with personal information removed, from 1,040 operations I performed from March 2023 to October 2026. Of the 119 that the surgical record classified as hardware removal, I analyzed 103 after excluding 16, such as removal of foreign bodies, calcium or loose bodies in a joint. The interval calculation is based on the 28 patients for whom both the fixation and the removal were confirmed for the same person. Because these are one doctor's records, please treat them as reference material rather than a general standard. This article is general information, and treatment must be decided through an examination. References Vos DI, Verhofstad MHJ. t: Gouty tophus of the knee
s: A case of a knee tophus in a 56-year-old man that grew for three years until it was about to break through the skin. Covers the MRI and surgical findings, the chalk-like urate crystals, when surgery is needed and wound care, and urate-lowering therapy and target uric acid levels after surgery.
k: gout tophus tophi gouty tophus knee lump uric acid urate crystals allopurinol prepatellar bursitis
b: Knee Gouty tophus of the knee Hee Seung Nam, MD, Orthopedic Surgeon · November 4, 2026 A 56-year-old man came in with a lump on the front of his left knee. He already had gout, and he said the lump had appeared three years earlier and kept growing. The front of the kneecap was red and swollen, and it hurt when pressed. A small wound had even formed in the middle of the thinned skin, so the lump was about to burst out. Before surgery. The front of the kneecap is red and swollen, and a small wound has formed in the middle of the thinned skin. Axial MRI taken at another hospital. A lump made of several clustered masses is seen under the skin in front of the kneecap. MRI: a mass covering the front of the kneecap The MRI he brought from another hospital showed a large mass under the skin in front of the kneecap (patella). Its inside was uneven, like several small masses clustered together. When a lump like this appears around a joint in someone with gout, a tophus is the first thing to suspect. Still, what a lump really is becomes certain only after it is removed and examined under the microscope. Knee MRI taken from several directions. The arrows mark the edges of the lump covering the front of the kneecap. Surgery: a mass that looked as if chalk dust had been ground into it The lump was about to break through the skin and it was painful, so we decided to remove it surgically. The skin over a tophus is thin and has poor blood supply, so the wound can be slow to heal after surgery; I explained this to him before the operation. The removed tophus. It measured 6.5 × 5.5 × 3.5 cm. It was a tophus. The first thing that catches the eye is the chalk-white or pale yellow material embedded throughout the tissue. These are urate crystals , formed as uric acid that had circulated in the blood for years built up and hardened. This look, as if dry chalk dust or plaster had been ground in, is the most distinctive feature of a tophus. The red, irregular tissue surrounding the white masses is chronic inflammatory tissue, formed as the body treats the urate crystals as foreign material and attacks them without end. As urate crystals grow they can burrow into nearby ligaments, the joint capsule and even bone, so in the photo the edges are not smooth but tangled with the surrounding tissue. A tophus this large means the problem has gone beyond pain: the urate mass has begun to damage the tissue around it. Pathology showed fine needle-shaped crystals surrounded by granulomatous inflammation and multinucleated giant cells, confirming a tophus. Because the lump was red and swollen we were also worried about infection, but the bacterial culture sent at the same time grew no bacteria. What is a tophus? Gout is a disease in which uric acid stays high in the blood for a long time and forms needle-shaped crystals that build up in joints and the tissues around them. When the crystals trigger inflammation, a joint suddenly swells and becomes very painful: a gout attack. Left untreated for a long time, the crystals clump into a mass, called a tophus . Tophi often form at the big toe, top of the foot, ankle, Achilles tendon, back of the elbow, fingers and the rim of the ear, and, as in this patient, they can also form in front of the knee. They usually grow slowly without pain, but when inflamed they become red, swollen and painful. As they grow, the skin thins and can burst, letting white chalky material leak out, and bacteria can enter the wound and cause infection. Gout is steadily increasing in Korea. A study of national health insurance data found that prevalence more than doubled, from 3.5 per 1,000 people in 2007 to 7.6 per 1,000 in 2015, and it was more common in men. Lumps in front of the knee The front of the kneecap has a bursa (a small fluid sac) just under the skin, so lumps often form there. They are often hard to tell apart by appearance alone, so the history, examination and ultrasound or MRI are considered together. Lumps in front of the knee Feature Prepatellar bursitis Common in people who kneel often. Feels like a soft fluid-filled sac Septic (bacterial) bursitis Red, hot and painful, sometimes with fever. Needs prompt antibiotic treatment Gouty tophus History of gout. Firm and lumpy; white material may show through the skin Soft tissue tumor Mostly benign, like a lipoma, but a lump that grows quickly, or is large and deep, needs a thorough work-up As in this patient, an inflamed tophus becomes red and swollen and can look like a bacterial infection. That is why, at surgery, the removed tissue is sent for both pathology and bacterial culture. When a tophus should be removed Most tophi slowly shrink when uric acid is lowered with medication. Surgery is considered in cases like these: When the skin has thinned and is about to break or has already broken, or when infection has set in When the tophus gets in the way of joint movement or wearing shoes, or presses on a nerve When the pain is severe When it needs to be confirmed whether the lump is a tophus or something else Wound care is central to tophus surgery. The skin over a tophus is thin and poorly supplied with blood, so wounds tend to heal slowly or reopen, and infection or other medical conditions increase complications. In a Taiwanese study of 303 tophus operations, leg wounds took an average of 19 days to heal, longer than arm wounds (13 days), and leg wounds with infection before surgery took even longer, 31 days. This is why operating before the skin breaks and becomes infected favors recovery. Surgery is a beginning, not the end Surgery removed the large tophus pressing on the knee, but that does not end the treatment. A tophus may look like a tumor, but it is not one; it is a mass caused by a problem with uric acid metabolism. Removing the visible mass leaves the uric acid stored throughout the body untouched, so if blood uric acid stays high, new tophi can form at other joints. Take urate-lowering medication consistently. The American College of Rheumatology strongly recommends starting urate-lowering therapy if there is even one tophus under the skin. Allopurinol is the first-line drug, started at a low dose and increased gradually. Keep to the target uric acid level. The basic goal is to keep serum uric acid below 6 mg/dL. For severe gout with tophi, EULAR (the European rheumatology alliance) recommends lowering it further, below 5 mg/dL, until the crystals dissolve. The lower the uric acid, the faster tophi shrink. In a study following 63 patients with tophi, the lower the serum uric acid during treatment, the faster the tophi shrank. The small crystals left in the tissue also need to be dissolved slowly this way for the surgical site to heal well and to prevent recurrence. Attacks can actually occur in the first months of treatment. This happens as stored crystals dissolve and are released, so for the first 3 to 6 months a preventive drug such as colchicine is taken as well. It is important not to stop urate-lowering medication because of an attack without talking to your doctor. Change daily habits too. Cut down on alcohol (especially beer), sugary drinks high in fructose, organ meats and red meat, and manage your weight. Diet alone, however, can hardly dissolve tophi that have already formed, so medication is the mainstay. In closing Gout is easy to dismiss as a disease that hurts for a while and then goes away. But if early pain is ignored, uric acid can clump into masses that try to break through the skin, as in this case, or damage joints and bone. If you feel an unexplained lump around your knee or toes, or the same spot swells and hurts again and again, see a specialist and get checked. If the skin over a lump turns red and thin, or white material shows through, it is best to be seen before it bursts. Surgery relieves pressure and pain right away and improves quality of life, but controlling gout properly requires steady medication together with dietary changes. After suffering for so long, I hope he can now return to daily life with a lighter step. This article is general medical information. Diagnosis and treatment can differ with the location and size of the lump, uric acid levels and other medical conditions, so please confirm through a medical consultation. t: Both shoulders hurt, but the cause was the liver: liver abscess and referred shoulder pain
s: A 66-year-old came in with pain in both shoulders and was diagnosed with a liver abscess by blood tests and CT. The case shows how liver and diaphragm problems can be felt as referred shoulder pain, and the warning signs that call for another cause.
k: shoulder pain referred pain liver abscess diaphragm
b: Shoulder Both shoulders hurt, but the cause was the liver: liver abscess and referred shoulder pain Hee Seung Nam, MD, Orthopedic Surgeon · September 16, 2026 A 66-year-old woman came in saying both of her shoulders had hurt for two weeks. When someone in her 60s comes with shoulder pain, I usually think first of frozen shoulder, a rotator cuff tear or calcific tendinitis. But her pain began not in the shoulder but in the liver . The shoulder X-rays were clean X-rays of both shoulders. Nothing is seen in the bones or joints that would explain the pain. On the X-rays of both shoulders I saw nothing in the bones or joints that would explain the pain. On examination she winced when I pressed the trapezius area above the shoulder, but the pattern was a little different from typical shoulder joint disease. When the X-ray is clean and the examination is ambiguous, it is common to move straight on to a shoulder injection or physical therapy. But wondering whether some other cause might be hiding, I ordered blood tests first. The signal in the blood tests Test Result What the test looks at CRP 25.60 The degree of inflammation somewhere in the body. It was greatly raised. ALT 102 An enzyme that leaks into the blood when liver cells are damaged GGT 223 An enzyme that rises when there is a problem in the liver or bile ducts (the channels that carry bile) LDH 280 An enzyme that rises when various tissues, including the liver, are damaged All values in the table are marked as abnormal because they exceeded the normal range of the laboratory that ran the test. Normal ranges differ slightly from lab to lab. CRP, the inflammation marker, was very high, and the liver enzymes were well beyond the normal range. It was a signal that this was not a simple joint problem but an internal medicine problem somewhere in the body that needed to be checked quickly. I immediately requested a gastroenterology consultation, and gastroenterology performed chest and abdominal CT. The cause found on CT: liver abscess Contrast-enhanced abdominal CT. At the tip of the arrow, the broad area at the front of the liver that is darker and mottled compared with its surroundings is the liver abscess. CT is viewed from the patient's feet looking up, so the left of the image is the patient's right. CT confirmed a liver abscess , a pocket of pus inside the liver. The patient was transferred straight to a tertiary hospital and began inpatient treatment. Why does a sore liver cause shoulder pain? The reason is referred pain . Referred pain is the phenomenon of feeling pain in a different part of the body, away from where the real problem is. A well-known example is the pain in the left arm or jaw during a heart attack. The pocket of pus and inflammation at the top of the liver irritate the diaphragm just above. Sensory signals from the diaphragm (especially its central part) travel along the phrenic nerve up to levels 3–5 of the cervical spinal cord (C3–C5). The sensory nerves for the skin over the top of the shoulder and trapezius (mainly C4) enter the spinal cord at the same levels. The brain mistakes the signal for one coming from the familiar shoulder area and feels that the shoulder hurts . Figure. A simplified drawing of how diaphragmatic referred pain works. For that reason, problems around the liver, gallbladder and diaphragm can show up as pain at the tip of the right shoulder or along the ridge between neck and shoulder. The trapezius area that hurt in this patient also overlaps the region served by the C4 nerve. The same thing happens on the left: when the left diaphragm is irritated, for example by a spleen injury, and the left shoulder hurts, it is called Kehr's sign . The liver is on the right, so it usually shows up as right shoulder pain. Why this patient had pain on both sides is hard to say for certain, but we can consider the possibility that the inflammation was widespread or that a systemic inflammatory response was also at work. Such cases are reported steadily. In a Korean case published in the Korean Journal of Pain, a 31-year-old man who improved after a bursa injection for right shoulder pain returned three weeks later with right upper abdominal pain and fever and was diagnosed with a liver abscess. An American emergency medicine journal also published a case in which multiple liver abscesses were found in a 92-year-old who came with pain in the right shoulder, flank and upper abdomen. It means that pain easing briefly after an injection does not necessarily mean the cause has been solved. What kind of disease is a liver abscess? A liver abscess is a disease in which bacteria enter the liver and form a pocket of pus. It can arise through bile duct disease such as gallstones, bacteria can enter from the intestine through the bloodstream, and in many cases no cause is found. It is more likely the older you are and with diabetes or weakened immunity. In Korea, Taiwan and elsewhere in Asia, Klebsiella pneumoniae is the main causative organism. A liver abscess due to this organism can rarely cause an “invasive liver abscess syndrome” that spreads to other organs such as the eye (endophthalmitis), the meninges of the brain or the lungs, so quick diagnosis and treatment are important. The typical symptoms are fever and abdominal pain, but because symptoms and blood test findings are not specific, it is sometimes mistaken for another disease at first. Diagnosis is by ultrasound or CT, which can confirm it in more than 90%. Treatment is usually 2–6 weeks of antibiotics, and when the abscess is large, percutaneous drainage, in which a thin tube is placed through the skin to drain the pus. Abscesses smaller than 3–5 cm are sometimes treated with antibiotics alone. Shoulder pain: when to suspect other causes What I want to stress first is that most shoulder pain is a problem of the shoulder joint and tendons . Internal organs are rarely the cause. But if you have features like those below, we should look at the whole body, not only the shoulder. Feature A problem of the shoulder itself Referred pain from an internal organ Relation to movement Hurts with specific movements; raising or turning the arm is often difficult Pain does not change much when the shoulder moves Accompanying symptoms Usually confined to the shoulder and arm Fever, loss of appetite, upper abdominal pain, shortness of breath, cold sweats and so on Test X-ray, ultrasound and MRI often show the cause Shoulder tests are normal, and the cause shows up on blood tests or chest and abdominal imaging Please be sure to tell me at your visit if: You have a fever, chills or cold sweats You have lost weight for no reason, or have been treated for cancer Shoulder pain gets worse when you breathe deeply or cough Your upper abdomen hurts, it gets worse after a fatty meal, or your eyes or skin have turned yellow The pain continues even when you rest the shoulder, and does not improve with shoulder treatment If you have tightness in the chest with pain spreading to the left shoulder, arm or jaw and cold sweats, it may be a heart problem. In that case do not wait for an appointment; call 119 (emergency services) right away. Items such as fever, weight loss and a history of cancer are also listed as warning signs that call for further tests in the British Medical Journal (BMJ) primary care guidance on shoulder pain. In closing If the shoulder X-ray is normal but the pattern of pain is not typical, causes outside the shoulder should also be considered. Problems of the liver, gallbladder and diaphragm can be felt as pain at the top of the shoulder through the phrenic nerve (C3–C5) . In this patient a simple blood test showed abnormal inflammation and liver markers, which led to a quick CT diagnosis of liver abscess and then to treatment. If fever, weight loss, pain that worsens with breathing, or upper abdominal pain come with it, please be sure to mention it at your visit. I am a doctor who looks at shoulders, but I try not to look only at the shoulder. I wish the patient a speedy recovery. This article is general medical information based on a single case. t: A 'pop' in the knee on a downhill walk: a radial meniscus tear and arthroscopic repair
s: MRI, arthroscopic repair and postoperative rehabilitation of a radial meniscus tear diagnosed after a knee twist while walking downhill.
k: knee meniscus cartilage tear arthroscopy root repair
b: Knee A 'pop' in the knee on a downhill walk: a radial meniscus tear and arthroscopic repair Hee Seung Nam, MD, Orthopedic Surgeon · October 28, 2026 Many people hurt a knee unexpectedly while walking or hiking and come to the hospital. Today I introduce a case of a 'radial tear of the meniscus' for which surgery is actively considered. Patient case and diagnosis He is a 54-year-old man. He twisted his knee going downhill, felt a 'pop' with severe pain, and came in. The pain continued afterward and he could not walk normally. The McMurray test, which checks for a meniscus injury, was clearly positive and the pain was severe, so I took an MRI right away to confirm the exact cause. MRI findings Knee MRI; the arrow marks the meniscus tear Another MRI slice of the same patient MRI confirmed a radial tear of the meniscus. The meniscus of the knee spreads body weight and absorbs shock. Its fibers are arranged in a circular direction and resist the pressure on the knee (hoop tension); a radial tear splits across these fibers. It is like a rubber band that has snapped, and if left alone the meniscus can lose its shock-absorbing function. It is known to have a worse outlook than other tear patterns and can bring on degenerative arthritis early even at a young age, so where possible I consider restoring it by repair. The arthroscopic procedure Before repair, the arthroscopic view showing the radial tear After repair, sutured with a double-arm needle Looking inside the knee with the arthroscope, the radial tear, in which the meniscus was split from the inside toward the outside, was clear, just as on MRI. A split meniscus must be fixed firmly back in place to regain its original function. After bringing the opened edges together precisely, I sutured them with a double-arm needle. I focused on restoring the anatomy so that the torn meniscal fibers could regain their original tension. Rehab after surgery In a radial tear the repaired site is under a lot of force from body weight trying to pull it open again. That is why care in the first 4 to 6 weeks is especially important. What follows is a general example and can vary with the tear pattern and surgical method. Up to 4 weeks after surgery (protection and healing) : wear a knee brace and walk on crutches without putting the foot down. The angle of knee bending is also usually limited to within 90 degrees so as not to stress the repair. 4 to 6 weeks (partial weight bearing) : with the brace on, begin practicing putting weight on the foot gradually, starting from the toes, and increase the bending angle little by little. After 6 weeks (full weight bearing and strengthening) : remove the brace and crutches and practice normal walking. Build up the thigh muscle weakened after surgery (the quadriceps) with a stationary bike and light strengthening. Serious exercise such as jogging or hiking is tried in stages, usually after 3 to 6 months depending on recovery. In closing A damaged meniscus often has trouble healing on its own. A radial tear in particular can lead to rapid progression of arthritis if left, so treatment that saves the original meniscus wherever possible is important. If the pain does not settle after a 'pop' in the knee, I recommend seeing an orthopedist without delay. If you have questions, please write to doctornhs@naver.com . This article is general information. Surgical results and recovery time differ from person to person with the tear pattern, age and activity level, and the treatment method must be decided through an examination. t: A meniscus root tear seen through the arthroscope, and how it is tied back
s: What a meniscus root tear really looks like inside the knee, explained with arthroscopic photos before and after transtibial pull-out root repair.
k: knee meniscus cartilage tear arthroscopy root repair
b: Knee A meniscus root tear seen through the arthroscope, and how it is tied back Hee Seung Nam, MD, Orthopedic Surgeon · October 30, 2026 In the previous article ( If you heard a 'pop' on the stairs: meniscus root tear ) I compared the 'root' of the meniscus to the iron hoop on a wooden barrel. Today I want to show arthroscopic pictures of a knee in which that hoop has broken. The images are part of the records of a patient I operated on, chosen so that no one can be identified. The 'torn root' seen inside the knee Image 1 Before repair. The back end of the medial meniscus has come away from where it should be attached to the bone, leaving a gap. The rounded surface at the top of the arthroscopic screen is the end of the thighbone, and the bottom is the meniscus resting on the shinbone. Normally the back end of the meniscus should be firmly attached to the center of the shinbone, but in this knee that spot is empty and the end of the meniscus hangs ragged. It can be diagnosed on MRI too, but seeing it with the arthroscope makes it immediately clear why people say the 'root has been pulled out.' In this state, when weight is applied the meniscus is pushed outward and cannot act as a cushion. How is it tied back? This patient did not have severe arthritis, so I performed a root repair to reattach the root to its original place. In brief, the method is as follows. Clean up the damaged tissue at the end of the detached meniscus and at the bone site where it was originally attached. Pass strong sutures through the end of the meniscus several times. Drill a small tunnel from the front of the shinbone to the site of the original root. Pull the sutures down through the tunnel to draw the end of the meniscus back into place, then tie them over a small metal button on the front of the shinbone to fix them. Image 2 The sutures passed through. The blue sutures are threaded through the end of the meniscus, and they will be pulled into the bone tunnel. After the repair is complete Image 3 After repair. The end of the meniscus has been pulled back to its original root site and reattached to the bone. When the sutures are pulled and fixed, the end of the meniscus is drawn into the empty spot and attached. It is as if the broken end of the hoop had been driven back into the barrel. Only then can the meniscus regain its ability to hold up when weight is applied (hoop tension). But attaching it in the operating room is not the end. It takes time for the pulled-down root to actually settle into the bone. That is why for about a month after surgery I tell patients to use crutches without putting weight on the leg, and to avoid deep knee bending for several months. Half of the result of surgery depends on how well this period is respected. Why I show the photographs We often hear that “the meniscus is torn,” but it is hard to imagine what that looks like inside the knee. If you see the torn site and the repaired site directly, I think it will be a little easier to feel why you should not dismiss it as “a bit better,” and why the crutch period after surgery has to be kept. Not every root tear can be repaired this way. If arthritis is far advanced or the legs are strongly bowed, I consider other treatments. The treatment choices are laid out in If you heard a 'pop' on the stairs: meniscus root tear . This article is general medical information, and the surgical method and rehab schedule can vary with the condition of the knee and the hospital. If you have symptoms, please consult an orthopedic specialist. It contains surgical photographs. References Lee DW, Ha JK, Kim JG. Medial Meniscus Posterior Root Tear: A Comprehensive Review . Knee Surg Relat Res . 2014;26(3):125–134. Moon HS, Choi CH, Jung M, et al. Medial Meniscus Posterior Root Tear: How Far Have We Come and What Remains? Medicina . 2023;59(7):1181.

t: If you heard a 'pop' on the stairs: meniscus root tear
s: A 'pop' behind the knee when squatting or going down stairs. A meniscus root tear is easy to dismiss because the pain eases after a few days.
k: knee meniscus cartilage tear arthroscopy root repair
b: Knee If you heard a 'pop' on the stairs: meniscus root tear Hee Seung Nam, MD, Orthopedic Surgeon · October 30, 2026 There is something I hear often in clinic. “I squatted down while working in the field and felt a 'pop' behind my knee. It hurt terribly for a few days, but now it is a little better.” I hear this especially from women in their 50s and 60s. And it is the “a little better” that worries me most. When an MRI is taken, a good many of them have a meniscus root tear . What is the 'root' of the meniscus? Inside the knee, between the thighbone and the shinbone, there are two crescent-shaped menisci, one on the inner side and one on the outer side. They are cushions that absorb shock and spread the load when weight is applied. Both ends of this crescent are firmly tied to the shinbone, and this part is called the root . Think of the iron hoop around a wooden barrel. Just as the ends of the hoop must be fastened for the barrel not to spread apart, the meniscus holds up under weight without being pushed outward only if its roots are attached. Normal: the roots at both ends are firmly tied down Posterior root tear of the medial meniscus: the hoop has come undone and is pushed outward from its original position (dotted line) Diagram of the knee seen from above (top of the shinbone). The red dots are where the meniscus roots attach to the bone. Why does it tear with a 'pop'? In young people, meniscus tears often come from a large force during sports. A tear of the posterior root of the medial meniscus, by contrast, often happens after middle age, in a meniscus already weakened bit by bit, during a very minor movement . When getting up from a squat When going down stairs or a downhill slope When sitting cross-legged, or just walking The 'pop' sound or feeling that patients remember is this very moment. Afterward the back or inner side of the knee hurts, especially going down stairs. Why “it's better, so it must be fine” is dangerous The severe pain of the first few weeks usually settles. That is why many people let it pass. The problem is that changes continue inside the knee in the meantime. A meniscus with a torn root is like a barrel whose hoop has come off. The shape remains, but it cannot bear the load and is pushed out of the joint. Biomechanical studies regard a completely torn root as a state similar to removing the whole meniscus . When bone and cartilage strike each other directly where the cushion has gone, the following can happen. Degenerative arthritis progresses faster than expected Tiny stress fractures form just under the bone surface and the pain suddenly becomes severe The time at which an osteotomy or knee replacement is needed comes sooner How is it diagnosed? The meniscus is not visible on a plain X-ray. The X-ray is used to check the joint space, the alignment of the leg and the degree of arthritis, and the root tear itself is diagnosed with MRI . On MRI you can see that the place where the root should be looks empty, or that the meniscus has been pushed out of the joint. If back-of-the-knee pain continued after a 'pop,' I recommend being examined at least once even if the pain has eased. The time when there are the most treatment choices is right after the injury. How is it treated? Not every root tear is operated on. Treatment differs by age, how far the arthritis has advanced and whether the leg is bowed. Condition of the knee Treatment mainly considered Little arthritis, with fairly straight leg alignment Meniscus root repair : the torn root is tied with sutures and pulled through a small tunnel in the bone to be fixed again Arthritis is not severe, but the bowlegged alignment is clear Osteotomy plus root repair : shifts the weight concentrated on the inner side outward to protect the repaired root Arthritis is already far advanced Conservative treatment such as pain control and exercise therapy, and if needed joint replacement (partial or total) Older patients, or when surgery is difficult Medication, injections, strengthening exercises, weight management, temporary use of crutches In the past, partial meniscectomy, cutting out the torn part, was often done, but studies showing that it does not stop progression of arthritis in root tears have appeared and it is rarely recommended now. For a knee in which the root can be fixed, the principle is to reattach rather than cut out . What about after surgery? A root repair needs time for the reattached site to heal. It differs by hospital and surgical method, but usually for a little over a month after surgery you use crutches and do not put weight on the leg. Deep knee-bending movements are also restricted for a period. I tell patients to avoid squatting and sitting cross-legged for several months or more. Repair does not stop arthritis completely. But there are many reports that by helping the meniscus act as a cushion again it slows arthritis and helps delay knee replacement. What you can do for your knees starting today Cut down on squatting and sitting cross-legged : deeply bent positions put the most strain on the back root of the meniscus. Use a low stool for fieldwork or hand-washing laundry. Take the elevator rather than the stairs : the load is especially great going down. Thigh strengthening exercises : if the muscle at the front of the thigh is strong, the shock reaching the knee is reduced. Weight management : studies suggest that losing 1 kg lowers the load on the knee by about 4 kg when walking. In closing Going through my surgical photo folders, I found far more meniscus root tear cases than I expected. A good many of them were patients who said, “it hurt at first, but it got better so I just carried on.” If you heard a 'pop' behind your knee and going down stairs has been uncomfortable since, have it checked once even if the pain has eased. Even for the same knee, the treatment differs depending on when it is found. This article is general medical information, and diagnosis and treatment can differ with the individual's condition. t: The first signal your bones send: osteopenia
s: What to check and how to manage osteopenia found on a health checkup, summarizing the author's op-ed for Bridge Economy.
k: osteoporosis osteopenia bone density weak bones
b: Fracture & Bone The first signal your bones send: osteopenia Hee Seung Nam, MD, Orthopedic Surgeon · October 29, 2026 October 20 is World Osteoporosis Day. Osteoporosis has no obvious symptoms in its early stage, so many people learn they have it only after a fracture. That is why a finding of 'osteopenia' on a health checkup is a first warning sign that should not be ignored. What is osteopenia? Osteopenia is the stage before osteoporosis, a state in which bone density is lower than normal but has not yet reached the criteria for osteoporosis. It is classified by the T-score of a bone density test as follows. T-score Diagnosis -1.0 or above Normal Below -1.0 and above -2.5 Osteopenia -2.5 or below Osteoporosis Not all osteopenia progresses to osteoporosis. But bone density outside the normal range means the bones have begun to weaken. Even with the same osteopenia, fracture risk differs greatly with age and the risk factors below. A history of fracture A family history of hip fracture in a parent Long-term steroid use Coexisting conditions such as rheumatoid arthritis Smoking and drinking What to check after the diagnosis Look back at past fractures. If you have ever broken a wrist, spine or hip just from falling from standing height (a fragility fracture), it should not be written off as a simple accident. Even if bone density is in the osteopenia range, a confirmed fragility fracture of the spine or hip allows a diagnosis of osteoporosis and treatment, and medication is also considered when fracture risk is high. Look at the trend in bone density. A single T-score shows only the present state. The amount of decline compared with earlier tests, menopausal status, medications and coexisting conditions should be reviewed together. Results differ with the equipment and the site measured, so rather than fretting over changes in the decimal point, it is better to set the timing of follow-up tests according to your individual risk. Prevention in daily life Diet : rather than relying on a single calcium supplement, eat a balanced diet that includes calcium, vitamin D and good-quality protein. Exercise : steadily combine weight-bearing exercise such as walking with strength and balance exercise. Preventing falls : in older people, not falling is as important as strengthening the bones. Clear away slippery floors, thresholds and dim lighting, and be especially careful in wet bathrooms. In closing Osteopenia is not a result that says 'it's not osteoporosis yet, so it's fine'; it is closer to a preliminary warning that you must manage the risk of osteoporosis and fractures going forward. Rather than treating after a fracture, checking risk factors and protecting the bones from the osteopenia stage is the starting point of lifelong bone health. This article summarizes a piece I contributed to Bridge Economy [Expert Column], “The first signal your bones send, 'osteopenia'… do strength exercise and check bone density” (October 13, 2026; in Korean): link . This article is general information. Interpreting bone density results and whether to treat depend on age, fracture history and coexisting conditions, so please confirm through an examination. t: How should a child's clavicle fracture be treated?
s: A case of a 12-year-old's displaced clavicle fracture treated with closed reduction without an incision and a figure-of-eight bandage: why children's clavicle fractures differ from adults' (thick periosteum and strong remodeling), before-and-after reduction images, healing from 1 week to 3 months, and the lump (callus) that can be felt.
k: clavicle fracture child pediatric closed reduction figure-of-eight callus
b: Fracture How should a child's clavicle fracture be treated? Hee Seung Nam, MD, Orthopedic Surgeon · November 5, 2026 A child's clavicle fracture is different from an adult's Clavicle fractures in children and adolescents have very distinctive features compared with adults. The biggest are an excellent ability to form bone and a thick periosteum , the membrane covering the bone. A child's periosteum is much thicker and tougher than an adult's, so even when the bone breaks it acts as a hinge (periosteal hinge) that keeps the broken ends from tearing badly through the surrounding tissue. Thanks to this, good results can be expected from treatment without surgery even when a child's clavicle fracture is somewhat displaced. Rather than forcing an open operation, the ideal approach is to protect the environment around the bone so the child's own healing ability can work to the full. A 12-year-old's clavicle fracture A 12-year-old boy seen recently shows this well. He came in with a left clavicle fracture, and front and cephalic tilt (cephalic oblique) X-rays clearly showed the outer hard layer (cortex) broken and displaced. It was not a case that absolutely required surgery, such as bone pressing on the skin or an open fracture, but I judged that treatment to reduce the displacement was needed. Front X-ray on arrival. The left clavicle is broken and displaced. The displacement is also visible on the cephalic tilt view. Aligning without an incision: closed reduction In the operating room, while watching on a real-time fluoroscope (C-arm), the bone was aligned by hand without opening the skin: a closed reduction . Before reduction After reduction. The cortex is continuous again. Comparing before and after, the displaced ends found their place and the cortex became smoothly continuous. It is hard to call it a 100% perfect reduction like fixation with metal, but aligning it without an incision is very meaningful. Opening the skin to expose the fracture damages the tiny blood vessels around the bone and washes away the fracture hematoma , which is rich in bone-forming factors and stem cells. A reduction without an incision keeps this natural healing environment intact. From one week to three months: how the bone heals Worried that the bone might slip again if X-rays were taken right after reduction, we took the next X-ray one week later. Fortunately, the cortex remained continuous on both the front and tilt views. 1 week, front view 1 week, tilt view. The cortex remains continuous. 2 weeks, front view 2 weeks, tilt view. 3 weeks, front view 3 weeks, tilt view. New bone bridging the break (callus) appears and is getting denser. 4 weeks, front view 4 weeks, tilt view. The callus is denser and the bone is joining in a rounded shape. 6 weeks. Much of the lower cortex has joined. 3 months. The bone has healed (union). Around 3 to 4 weeks, as the bone heals, callus forms at the fracture and may be felt as a lump under the skin. This shows the bone is healing well, and as the child grows the bone is reshaped (remodeling) and gradually flattens over months to years, so there is no need to worry. To prevent further displacement and help stable healing, this boy kept a figure-of-eight bandage for three weeks starting one week after the reduction. In closing A child's clavicle has a thick periosteum and strong bone-forming ability, so most heal well without surgery even when somewhat displaced. When displacement is large, a closed reduction without an incision can correct the position while protecting the healing environment. The lump (callus) felt during healing is normal and mostly flattens as the child grows. Surgery is considered, however, when bone has broken or threatens to break through the skin, when nerve or blood vessel injury is suspected, or in late adolescents with severe displacement and shortening. I believe conservative treatment that makes the most of a child's natural healing power is the safest and best choice for long-term results in young patients. This article is general medical information. Treatment can differ with the fracture pattern and the child's age and condition, so please confirm through a medical consultation. t: If the leg with a hip replacement breaks: periprosthetic fracture and revision surgery
s: A periprosthetic fracture of the femur around a hip replacement, explained through the real case of a 90-year-old patient: the Vancouver classification, why revision is chosen for a B2 fracture with a loose stem, surgery with a long modular stem and a grip plate, and aftercare and prevention.
k: periprosthetic fracture hip replacement hemiarthroplasty bipolar revision Vancouver B2 modular stem thigh bone femur
b: Hip & Pelvis If the leg with a hip replacement breaks: periprosthetic fracture and revision surgery Hee Seung Nam, MD, Orthopedic Surgeon · November 3, 2026 Hip replacement is a good operation that relieves pain and gets people walking again. But years later, after a fall or as the bone weakens, the thigh bone that holds the implant can break. This is called a periprosthetic fracture . This is the story of a patient around 90 years old who had previously had a right hip hemiarthroplasty (bipolar). The thigh bone around the implant stem broke, and we performed a revision: the old stem was removed and replaced with a longer one. In this operation I used a modular revision stem for the first time, and I describe that experience here too. What is a periprosthetic fracture? As the name says, it is a fracture of the bone around (peri-) an implant (prosthesis). With hip replacements it usually occurs in the thigh bone (femur) that holds the metal stem. Falls: the most common cause. In older people with osteoporosis, even a minor fall can cause a break. Where stress concentrates: force gathers where the stiff metal stem meets softer bone, especially at the tip of the stem. Weakened bone: over time the bone around the stem can thin or the stem can loosen, leaving the bone vulnerable to small impacts. This is not a minor fracture. In a study of 328 periprosthetic femur fractures across 16 Scottish hospitals in 2019, the average patient age was 79 and one-year mortality was 20.8%. That is lower than for ordinary hip fractures (29%), but 2.7 times higher than in the general population of the same age. That is why early diagnosis and treatment that gets patients up again quickly matter. How treatment is decided: the Vancouver classification Periprosthetic fractures are grouped by the Vancouver classification . The key questions are where the fracture is and whether the implant stem is still firmly fixed . Type A Greater or lesser trochanter Stem left in place; small fixation if needed Type B1 Around the stem; stem well fixed Fracture fixed with plate and cables Type B2 Around the stem; stem loose Revision with a long stem ± fracture fixation Type B3 Loose stem + poor bone stock Revision with bone augmentation; major reconstruction Type C Well below the stem tip Stem left in place; fracture fixed alone A simplified drawing of the Vancouver classification. Red lines are fractures; the orange dotted line means the stem has loosened. This patient had a type B2 fracture. Type B, around the stem, is the most common and the hardest to judge. If the stem is firm (B1), only the broken bone is fixed with a plate and cables. If the stem is loose (B2), fixing the bone alone leaves the stem wobbling, so the rule is revision: remove the stem and replace it with a longer one that passes the fracture and reaches healthy bone . If too little bone remains (B3), a larger reconstruction is needed. This patient: a B2 fracture with a loose stem Preoperative front view. The bone on the outer side of the stem has split off in a long piece, and the fracture line runs down near the stem tip. Preoperative side view. With the bone around the stem broken, nothing is left to hold the stem. The X-ray showed the upper femur around the stem split lengthwise. With the bone that held the stem broken, the stem could no longer be considered stable. This is a Vancouver type B2 fracture. Preoperative CT. 3D images and several slices (yellow arrows) showed how far down the fracture ran and how many fragments there were, and we planned the operation from them. It is hard to tell from X-rays alone how far down the fracture runs, so we took a CT. The new stem must anchor in solid, unbroken bone well below the fracture, so this information is where surgical planning starts. Surgery: remove the stem, bind the bone, insert a longer stem Removing the old stem: the loose hemiarthroplasty stem was taken out. Reducing the broken bone: the greater trochanter (the bony bump on the outside of the hip) and the long split fragment on the outer side were put back in place, then bound with a grip plate that hooks over the trochanter, and cables. The hip muscles attach to the greater trochanter, so it has to heal well for the patient to walk without a limp. Inserting a long stem: a long revision stem was inserted past the fracture to anchor in the solid bone below. Bone graft and the joint: gaps in the bone were filled with graft, and because the cartilage on the pelvic side was in good shape, a hemiarthroplasty (bipolar) head was fitted again. Postoperative front view. The long stem passes the fracture into the bone below, and the greater trochanter and outer fragment are fixed with the grip plate and cables. Postoperative side view. The stem tip sits well below the fracture line, and the cables hold the split bone around the stem. Component What was used Role Revision stem Modular conical stem, distal length 155 mm, diameter 17 mm Anchors in solid bone below the fracture and carries body weight Proximal body 23 mm, length +10 mm Sets leg length and joint position separately Head 28 mm ceramic head + 50 mm bipolar Hemiarthroplasty, leaving the pelvic side as it is Plate Greater trochanteric grip plate (6 holes) Fixes the greater trochanter and outer fragment Cables 7 (3 attached to the plate, 4 free) Bind the split bone around the stem Bone graft 15 cc cancellous allograft Fills gaps to help the bone heal A modular stem, used for the first time What made this operation unusual was the use of Stryker's Restoration Modular system. It was my first time using it. An ordinary stem is a single piece. A modular stem is assembled from a separately chosen distal stem and proximal body . First, a long, fluted, conical distal stem is driven firmly into the unbroken femur to achieve fixation. Then a proximal body of the right length and orientation is chosen to set leg length and joint position. In a periprosthetic fracture the upper bone is broken, so the usual bony landmarks for judging height are gone. Being able to get fixation from below and set leg length from above, separately, suits this situation well. Because the system was new to me, I measured stem length and diameter on X-rays several times before surgery, and during surgery I checked length and stability with trial components before inserting the final implants. There is evidence behind it. In a Mayo Clinic study of 44 patients with B2 and B3 fractures treated with this kind of modular conical stem and followed for an average of 4.5 years, 98% of fractures healed and 98% of stems were stably fixed. However, 11% needed reoperation for dislocation, a reminder that dislocation must be watched for after surgery. Does a B2 fracture always require changing the stem? Not always. Depending on the stem type and fracture pattern, there are reports that precise fixation of the bone alone can be enough. But the evidence from studies comparing the two is still weak. In this patient, the bone that held the stem was itself shattered, so we judged it unwise to leave the stem in place. Care after surgery For older patients the most important goal is getting out of bed as early as possible . Long bed rest quickly brings pneumonia, blood clots, pressure sores and loss of strength. Weight bearing: increased gradually with a walker, depending on the fixation and bone quality, and advanced as X-rays show the bone healing. Preventing dislocation: avoid bending the hip deeply or crossing the leg inward. Details are in the discharge guide after hip replacement . Osteoporosis treatment: keep up bone density testing and medication to prevent the next fracture ( osteopenia column ). Prevention is the best treatment Fall prevention: non-slip mats, bathroom grab bars and a night light, plus a cane or walker if needed. Osteoporosis care: check bone density regularly and keep up calcium, vitamin D and medication. Strength exercise: regular training of the hip and thigh muscles improves balance and lowers the risk of falls. Regular checkups: even after a hip replacement, have regular X-rays to make sure the stem has not loosened. When to come in right away: if, after a fall, the thigh of the replaced hip hurts or you cannot put weight on the leg, see a doctor right away. In closing Periprosthetic fractures mostly result from falls, and in older patients they can be life-threatening. Treatment depends on where the fracture is and whether the stem is firm . For a B2 fracture with a loose stem, revision to a long stem is the rule. A modular stem lets the surgeon get fixation from below and set leg length from above separately, which helps when the bone is broken. Fall prevention and osteoporosis treatment are the surest ways to prevent it. This article is general medical information. Treatment can differ depending on the fracture pattern, bone condition and overall health, so please confirm through a medical consultation. References Duncan CP, Masri BA. t: Proximal humerus fracture-dislocation: comparing two cases
s: A comparison of two patients whose shoulders dislocated forward while the top of the upper arm bone (proximal humerus) and the greater tuberosity broke. Covers why emergency surgery was done on a Friday evening, reduction and greater tuberosity repair, fixation with a plate and tension band sutures, and the risk of avascular necrosis.
k: proximal humerus fracture dislocation shoulder fracture shoulder dislocation greater tuberosity avascular necrosis plate
b: Shoulder Proximal humerus fracture-dislocation: comparing two cases Hee Seung Nam, MD, Orthopedic Surgeon · November 4, 2026 I recently operated on two patients in a row with a proximal humerus fracture-dislocation , in which the shoulder dislocates and the top of the upper arm bone breaks as well. Here I introduce and compare the two cases. First patient: arriving as Friday clinic was closing A 60-year-old woman came in with left shoulder pain after falling in her vegetable garden, just as Friday clinic was about to close. Sensation, movement and circulation in the lower arm were normal. X-ray. The humeral head has dislocated forward and the greater tuberosity has broken off. 3D CT. The dislocated humeral head and the shattered greater tuberosity fragments are clearly seen. Axial CT. The humeral head has dislocated in front of the shoulder socket (glenoid). Postoperative X-ray. The dislocation was reduced and fixed with a plate and screws. If the shoulder stays dislocated over the weekend, the risk rises that the blood supply to the humeral head is cut off and the bone dies ( avascular necrosis of the humeral head ), even if surgery is done later. So after the required fasting time, we operated that same evening. At surgery, the dislocated humerus was first put back in place (reduction). Then pulling the greater tuberosity fragment, which had been pushed backward, with strong sutures and stitching it took a long time; I managed it only by rotating the arm inward. Part of the greater tuberosity was missing, but the remaining fragments were gathered as much as possible and fixed together with tension band sutures . Postoperative CT. The joint surface is back in place. Postoperative axial CT. The greater tuberosity fragments were also gathered and fixed as much as possible. Second patient: a 55-year-old man who fell from a height A 55-year-old man injured his right shoulder falling from a height while doing maintenance work. Like the first patient he had both a fracture and a dislocation, but where the first dislocated forward, this one dislocated forward and downward . X-ray. The humeral head has dislocated forward and downward, and the greater tuberosity is broken. 3D CT. The detached greater tuberosity fragment is visible. Axial CT. The humeral head has left the socket. Postoperative X-ray. After reduction, it was fixed with a plate and screws. Likewise, reduction and internal fixation were done, and the greater tuberosity was gathered as much as possible with tension band sutures. Postoperative CT confirms that the greater tuberosity came together well. Postoperative CT of the second patient. The greater tuberosity came together well. Comparing the two cases Feature First patient Second patient Age and sex 60-year-old woman 55-year-old man How it happened Fell in a vegetable garden Fell from a height at work Direction of dislocation Forward Forward and downward Surgery Same-evening reduction, plate fixation, tension band suture of the greater tuberosity Reduction, plate fixation, tension band suture of the greater tuberosity What is a proximal humerus fracture-dislocation? The top of the upper arm bone consists of a ball-shaped head and two bumps beside it, the greater and lesser tuberosities. When this area breaks as the shoulder dislocates, it is called a fracture-dislocation. Risk of avascular necrosis: the vessels to the humeral head are thin and run close to the joint, so when a fracture and a dislocation occur together the blood supply is easily cut off. The longer it stays out, the worse, so it is reduced as soon as possible. The role of the greater tuberosity: the rotator cuff tendons that lift and rotate the arm attach to it. If it heals out of place, the arm catches or feels weak when raised, and shoulder function declines. Surgery is often recommended when it is displaced by 5 mm or more. No forceful reduction: forcing a dislocation with a fracture back into place can widen the fracture, so it is safer to check the fracture on X-ray and CT and reduce it under anesthesia. In closing In both cases, what mattered most was reducing the dislocated shoulder smoothly and restoring the greater tuberosity to its place. The greater tuberosity is where the rotator cuff tendons attach, so if it is not restored, shoulder function inevitably declines after surgery. In both patients, the fragmented greater tuberosity was gathered as much as possible and strong tension band sutures were added, achieving stable fixation. Proximal humerus fracture-dislocations call for a flexible approach depending on how the injury happened, the patient's age and when they arrive. When a dislocation is present, prompt reduction and surgery are needed to reduce the risk of avascular necrosis. For final functional recovery, the greatest effort should go into restoring the greater tuberosity. This article is general medical information. Treatment can differ with the fracture pattern and the patient's condition, so please confirm through a medical consultation. References Neer CS 2nd. Displaced proximal humeral fractures. I. t: Getting to know robotic partial knee replacement
s: An overview of partial (unicompartmental) knee replacement, which replaces only the damaged part when arthritis affects one compartment of the knee: who it suits, robotic-arm surgery, recovery and care, pros and cons, and comparison with total knee replacement, with a real case.
k: partial knee replacement unicompartmental knee arthroplasty UKA robotic MAKO knee arthritis
b: Knee Getting to know robotic partial knee replacement Hee Seung Nam, MD, Orthopedic Surgeon · November 5, 2026 The knee joint has three compartments: inner (medial), outer (lateral), and behind the kneecap (patellofemoral). A partial knee replacement replaces the cartilage and bone of only one compartment when just that part is worn; it is also called unicompartmental knee arthroplasty (UKA). Unlike a total knee replacement (TKA), which replaces the whole joint, it keeps the healthy parts and ligaments, preserving natural movement as much as possible and allowing faster recovery. It is most often done for medial compartment arthritis, but can also be done for the lateral or patellofemoral compartment. When is it needed? Arthritis in only one compartment: degenerative or post-traumatic arthritis limited to the inner or outer side of the knee The rest of the joint and the ligaments are healthy: in particular, the anterior cruciate ligament must work properly. Pain not relieved by conservative treatment: medication, injections and physical therapy no longer control the pain and daily life is difficult Relatively young, active patients: well suited to people in their 50s and 60s who are active and want to avoid a total knee replacement. If arthritis has spread to other compartments or the leg is badly deformed, a partial knee replacement may not be suitable. Surgery with a robotic arm I perform partial knee replacement with a robotic arm (MAKO). A 3D plan tailored to the patient's knee is made from a preoperative CT, and during surgery the robotic arm helps cut the bone according to that plan. Anesthesia: spinal or general anesthesia. Incision: the knee is opened on the side of the damaged compartment (usually the inner side). The incision is smaller than for a total knee replacement. Checking the joint: the worn compartment, the other compartments and the anterior and posterior cruciate ligaments are checked again by eye and by hand. Cutting bone with the robotic arm: only the worn surfaces of the thigh bone and shin bone are cut precisely according to the CT plan. Trial components and balancing: trial implants are inserted to check alignment, stability and movement. Fixing the implant and closing: the metal (thigh bone side) and plastic (shin bone side) components are fixed with bone cement and the wound is closed. The operation usually takes 1 to 2 hours. A real case This patient's right knee had cartilage worn away in the medial compartment, with bone rubbing on bone. During surgery we confirmed that the lateral compartment and patellofemoral joint were healthy and that the anterior and posterior cruciate ligaments worked, then replaced only the medial compartment with the robotic arm. At the end of surgery the knee moved smoothly from 0 to 130 degrees. Postoperative front X-ray. The implant was placed only in the medial compartment. Postoperative side X-ray. The rest of the joint and the ligaments remain intact. Recovery and care 1 to 2 weeks after surgery: gradually put weight on the leg using a walker or crutches. Raise the leg to heart level to reduce swelling. 2 to 6 weeks: rehabilitation restores range of motion and strength. Most people return to daily life in this period. After 6 weeks: start light exercise such as walking and swimming; by 3 to 6 months most normal activities are possible. Manage swelling with ice and compression bandages, and keep strengthening the front thigh muscles (quadriceps). The implant is checked at outpatient visits 6 weeks, 3 months and 1 year after surgery. Pros and cons Pros: healthy joint and ligaments remain, so the knee moves naturally, and the small incision means faster recovery and a shorter hospital stay. It can be converted to a total knee replacement later if needed. Cons: it is possible only when arthritis is limited to one compartment, and over time the implant may wear or loosen, or arthritis may progress in other compartments, requiring a total knee replacement. Complications and precautions Wound infection, leg vein blood clots, implant wear or loosening, and arthritis progressing in other compartments can occur. Medication may be used to prevent clots; smokers should quit and people with excess weight benefit from losing it. Starting rehabilitation early after surgery is also important. Comparison with total knee replacement Item Partial knee replacement Total hip replacement Indication Arthritis in one compartment Arthritis in several compartments, severe deformity Movement Better preserves natural movement May be somewhat limited Recovery Fast (weeks to months) Relatively slow (months to a year) Durability Reported revision rates somewhat higher than total knee replacement Often lasts 15 to 20 years or more Best suited to Relatively young, active patients Older patients, damage in several compartments A study comparing about 100,000 matched patients from the UK joint registry found that partial knee replacement had fewer complications and deaths after surgery than total knee replacement, but a higher revision rate. It is best to choose with a specialist, considering joint condition, age and activity level. Returning to daily life Most people return to daily life within 6 to 12 weeks, and after 3 to 6 months light sports such as golf, swimming and cycling are possible. High-impact activities such as running and jumping can speed up implant wear and are best avoided. Regular rehabilitation exercise and weight control are the keys to making it last. In closing A partial knee replacement is a good treatment that can give both pain relief and natural movement to people with only one worn compartment. It is not right for everyone, however, so I recommend deciding after thorough discussion with more than one specialist. This article is general medical information. Treatment can differ with joint condition and individual circumstances, so please confirm through a medical consultation. References Liddle AD, Judge A, Pandit H, Murray DW.
