Lancet . 2014;384(9952):1437–1445.

t: A lump you can feel: lipoma or sarcoma?
s: Most lumps you can feel are benign, such as lipomas, but rarely one is a sarcoma. Warning signs by size, depth, growth rate and pain, the order of ultrasound, MRI and biopsy, and why a lump should not be cut out casually.
k: lump tumor lipoma sarcoma biopsy
b: Tumor A lump you can feel: lipoma or sarcoma? Hee Seung Nam, MD, Orthopedic Surgeon · October 31, 2026 “I felt a lump in my thigh in the shower. Could it be cancer?” It is a question I hear often in clinic. Let me start with the reassuring part. Lumps you can feel are mostly benign . Only very rarely a malignant tumor called a sarcoma is mixed in, and at first a sarcoma looks almost the same as a lipoma from the outside. What troubled me most while caring for bone and soft tissue tumor patients during residency was that the size of the later operation can change greatly depending on the order in which a lump was first investigated and treated. This article lays out how to tell lumps you need not worry about from lumps you must check. 99 of 100 lumps are benign According to a review in the BMJ, soft tissue tumors of the limbs are about 100 times more often benign than malignant . The most common is the lipoma, a lump of fat, followed by the ganglion cyst around joints, the epidermoid cyst under the skin and the schwannoma arising from nerves. Figure 1. The ratio of benign to malignant soft tissue lumps shown as dots. Benign lumps, including lipomas, are overwhelmingly common. A sarcoma is a malignant tumor that arises in connective tissue other than bone, such as muscle, fat, nerve, blood vessel and fibrous tissue. It is rare, about 1% of all adult cancers, and there are dozens of subtypes. The problem is that most are painless . Because it does not hurt, people assume “it must be a lipoma,” and often come to the hospital only after it has grown large. How deep it lies matters Under the skin there is a layer of fat, and beneath it the tough membrane that wraps the muscle, the fascia . Whether a lump is above or below the fascia is the first fork in the road. Figure 2. The layers under the skin. ① A shallow lump in the subcutaneous fat above the fascia is mostly benign, such as a lipoma. ② A deep lump within or between muscles below the fascia calls for a detailed work-up regardless of size. The ultrasound guidance of the British Sarcoma Group (BSG) explains that a fatty lump in the layer of fat just under the skin is rarely malignant even if it looks slightly unusual on ultrasound. Conversely, a lump deep below the fascia, or a lump that grew back after being removed, is more likely to be a sarcoma. Lumps to worry about: four signs The warning signs that UK and European sarcoma guidelines have in common are as follows. If even one applies, it is best to check with imaging. 5 cm or larger Be careful if it is bigger than a golf ball (about 4.3 cm). A typical lipoma in the subcutaneous fat may be an exception. Deep, below the fascia A lump within or between muscles needs to be checked regardless of size. Gradually getting bigger If you can feel it growing over weeks or months, it is the most important sign. Painful, or came back after removal A lump that has become painful, or that came back in the same spot after surgery, also needs to be checked. The UK National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) recommends that adults with a growing lump of unknown cause have an ultrasound within two weeks. The European Society for Medical Oncology (ESMO) guideline also recommends that a superficial lump larger than 5 cm, or a deep lump, be checked with imaging and biopsy. There are liposarcomas that look like lipomas Not every lump made of fat is a lipoma. Among fatty tumors that grow large in deep places, such as between thigh muscles, some are atypical lipomatous tumors (well-differentiated liposarcoma). They almost never spread elsewhere, but if removed incompletely they grow back and, rarely, can change into a more aggressive form. In a study by a German team that compared 113 fatty tumors with MRI and genetic testing, there was not a single atypical lipomatous tumor in the fat layer under the skin, and most lay between muscles. On MRI, septa thicker than 2 mm , areas that brighten with contrast and very large size were the suspicious findings, and the final confirmation is made by finding MDM2 gene amplification in tissue. Common lipoma Atypical lipomatous tumor, liposarcoma Location Often in the fat layer under the skin Between muscles, deep below the fascia Size Usually under 5 cm May grow to 10 cm or more MRI Uniform fat, thin septa Thick septa, nodules, contrast enhancement Treatment Simple removal if bothersome A planned operation, with follow-up needed There is an order to the tests Figure 3. The order of tests when a lump is found. If there are warning signs, MRI and biopsy come before surgery. Ultrasound : the first test. It shows the depth and size of the lump, its internal appearance and blood flow. A typical shallow lipoma or ganglion cyst can mostly be judged on ultrasound alone. MRI : if there are warning signs or the ultrasound finding is unclear, MRI is used to check the extent and nature of the tumor and its relation to nearby nerves and vessels. Biopsy : a bit of tissue is taken with a thick needle to confirm the diagnosis. Because the biopsy tract must also be removed with the tumor later, the principle is that the team that will do the final surgery plans where the needle goes in . In a study by the Musculoskeletal Tumor Society in the United States that analyzed 597 patients, when the biopsy was done somewhere other than a tumor treatment center, diagnostic errors and complications were 2 to 12 times more frequent. In 19% of all patients, treatment became more complicated because of biopsy problems, and there were 18 amputations that could have been avoided. Why “let's just take it out first” is dangerous Sometimes a small, soft lump is removed without imaging and the biopsy then shows a sarcoma. In a meta-analysis (2024) of such unplanned excisions, when a wide re-excision was done, about 60% still had tumor remaining , and the five-year local recurrence risk was higher than with planned surgery. To be fair, in this study there was no meaningful difference in overall survival. But to get rid of the remaining tumor you have to operate again much more widely than the first time, and radiation treatment is added in some cases. If sarcoma had been kept in mind and planned for from the start, it could have been done in one operation. That is why the principle is to get imaging first, before removing a lump that has warning signs . In closing Lumps you need not worry too much about : a lump just under the skin that is small and soft, has stayed the same size for years and does not hurt is mostly a lipoma. Even so, have it checked once with an examination and ultrasound. Lumps you must check : 5 cm or larger, deep below the fascia, getting bigger, painful or recurrent. If even one of these applies, check with ultrasound and MRI, and if needed have a biopsy by a team experienced in tumor treatment. The order matters : imaging, then biopsy, then surgery. Following this order alone can change the outcome of sarcoma treatment. This article is general medical information. The tests and treatment needed can differ with the location and size of the lump and the imaging findings, so please confirm through an examination. References Mannan K, Briggs TW. t: A surgeon's “I should have...” notes
s: A one-line memo added after a folder name when surgery is over. An orthopedic surgeon takes out a few of his own "I should have..." notes.
k: notes surgery records regrets
b: Notes A surgeon's “I should have...” notes Hee Seung Nam, MD, Orthopedic Surgeon · October 29, 2026 My computer has several hundred surgical photo folders. When an operation is finished I name the folder, and I have a habit of adding one line after the date and the name of the operation. “Should have...” “Look at...” “Next time, like this.” It is not written to show to anyone. It is a note to myself, left so I can open it again the night before the next operation. Today I want to take out a few of those notes. I have changed the details so that the patients cannot be identified. My PC › Surgical photos › 2023–2026 Case Notes Patellar fracture internal fixation — Be careful if it feels too tight. Be sure to look at the skyline view Medial meniscus posterior horn root tear — Should have just drilled the bone tunnel Periprosthetic femur fracture — Should have used a slightly smaller screw Arthroscopic rotator cuff repair — I think I did it well, in my own opinion There is always one line after the name of a surgical photo folder. Part of the actual folders, redrawn so that patients cannot be identified. 01 “Be careful if it feels too tight. Be sure to look at the skyline view” It was a patient with a broken kneecap (patella). The operation is to fit the broken fragments together and fix them with cannulated screws. The cannula placed along the path of the screw felt like it was biting tightly into the bone, and I took that feeling as a sign that it was “gripping well.” But on the post-operative images, the upper screw was touching the cartilage surface on the inner side of the kneecap. It was at an angle that could not be seen on the front and side images alone. If I had taken the skyline view, bending the knee and looking up at the kneecap from below, I would have known right away in the operating room. The note I left in the folder that day is two lines. A solid feeling in the hand is not always the right answer, and there is no harm in taking one more confirming image. 02 “Should have just drilled the bone tunnel” It was a patient with a torn root of the medial meniscus. The meniscus root is like an anchor that ties the meniscus to the bone, and when it is torn the meniscus cannot do its job. There are several ways to fix a root. I wrestled for a long time in the narrow space at the back of the knee trying to stitch the torn site as it was, and in the end I finished with another fixation device. The operation was done, but it would have been simpler if I had chosen from the start the method of cleaning up the damaged root, drilling a small tunnel in the bone and pulling the root down to fix it. The folder name also has a note that reads, “Don't force a stitch at the back.” It means that it matters far more to decide a second plan before surgery, “if this doesn't work, we go with that,” than to change plans in the middle of the operation. 03 “Should have used a slightly smaller screw” This was a patient who came with a broken thighbone near a knee that had been replaced. It is an operation in which the knee replacement already occupies the space, so there is not much room to place screws. The inner surface of the lower thighbone slopes more obliquely than you would think. I knew it in my head, but when it came to choosing a screw my hand went toward “the longer and thicker, the stronger.” Looking at the post-operative images, I thought that if I had considered that slope once more, a shorter, thinner screw would have been enough. The same folder also has a note: “Holding the top of the bone with the instrument is harder than it seems.” There is always a difference of a few degrees between the textbook anatomy drawing and the real patient's bone, and those few degrees can only be learned in the operating room. 04 “I think I did it well, in my own opinion” It is not only confessions. The day I arthroscopically repaired a small tear of the shoulder tendon (rotator cuff), I carefully wrote on the folder name, “I think I did it well, in my own opinion.” I added the words “in my own opinion” because I know the real verdict comes months later, from the patient's shoulder. There are also many folders where I wrote down tricks I learned from other surgeons. In ankle surgery, where to open the skin so as not to cut the ligament twice When inserting a rod for a hip fracture, which way to push the entry point Some tricks were used in the very next operation, and some are still waiting for the day they will be used again. In closing: why I took out these notes Patients facing surgery often ask, “How many times have you done this operation?” It is a good question. I would like to suggest one more to add to it: “What do you look at again after an operation is over?” The number of operations tells you the amount of experience, and the habit of looking back tells you whether that experience turns into skill. My “should have” notes are an embarrassing record, but they are also the surest way to make the next patient's operation a little better. This evening too, I will probably create a folder and write a line after it. Hee Seung Nam

t: Surgery is a last resort, not the worst option
s: Common worries when surgery comes up, and what to check before you decide.
k: surgery fear worry last resort
b: Notes Surgery is a last resort, not the worst option Hee Seung Nam, MD, Orthopedic Surgeon · December 24, 2025 When I explain while looking at an X-ray in clinic, I often hear this: "I heard you shouldn't cut into a joint. They say if you have surgery you can't walk." It is natural to fear surgery. I too use it sparingly and say that we should first do enough non-surgical treatment, such as exercise, medication and injections. Why does talk about surgery sound louder? People who recover well quietly return to daily life. Experiences with disappointing results, on the other hand, are talked about for a long time and travel far. So cases heard from people around you easily feel as though they represent the whole. Distrust of doctors who recommend surgery also plays a part. Ask before you decide How far have non-surgical treatments been tried in my present condition, and can more be expected from them? What is the purpose of the surgery, and what could get better? What could happen if I do not have surgery? What are the risks of complications and the length of rehab? What are the other options? You may be told that surgery is not needed, or you may be told to wait and watch. What matters is not to decide in advance "I'll never have surgery, no matter what," but to decide together, based on evidence, with the doctor who knows your condition best. Getting another specialist's opinion when needed is also a good approach. This article is general information. Treatment can differ with the individual's condition and lifestyle, so please confirm through an examination.

t: The tip of my finger won't straighten: tendinous mallet finger and skin-tendon fixation
s: Diagnosis and treatment of tendinous mallet finger, where only the tendon is torn, and the technique and six-week recovery of skin-tenodesis, shown with real photographs.
k: finger mallet finger fingertip tendon
b: Hand The tip of my finger won't straighten: tendinous mallet finger and skin-tendon fixation Hee Seung Nam, MD, Orthopedic Surgeon · October 15, 2026 One person came in after pulling hard on a towel and hearing a 'snap' at the tip of the little finger; the end joint then dropped downward and would not straighten on its own. Because the tip of the finger bends like the head of a hammer, it is called mallet finger . Did a piece of bone come off, or is only the tendon torn? The tendon that straightens the end joint of the finger (the extensor tendon) attaches to the back of the bone of the end segment. If the end joint is suddenly bent forcefully, this tendon tears, or the piece of bone to which the tendon attaches comes off with it. Type Condition Usual treatment Tendinous mallet finger Only the tendon is torn, with no bone injury The basic treatment is to keep wearing a splint that holds the end joint straight for at least 6 weeks Bony mallet finger A bone fragment with the tendon attached comes off A splint if the fragment is small and the joint is not displaced; surgery if the fragment is large or the joint is displaced Before surgery. The end segment (the bone at the top) droops downward, but there is no detached bone fragment. During surgery. The tendon that straightens the end joint was completely torn. This patient had no detached bone fragment on X-ray, so I diagnosed a tendinous mallet finger in which only the tendon is torn. If left untreated, the end joint stiffens in the bent position, and over time it can lead to a swan-neck deformity in which the middle joint bends backward. Most heal with a splint For a fresh tendinous mallet finger, a splint that holds the end joint straight is the basic treatment. A review by a Korean hand surgery team describes continuing to wear the splint for at least 6 weeks so the end joint does not bend, then wearing it only at night for about 2 more weeks. If the end joint is bent even once during this period, the healing tendon can pull apart again, so it is important to support the finger and keep it straight even when taking the splint off. Surgery is considered, though, for people whose job or life makes it hard to wear a splint for long, who have skin problems, whose finger droops again after splint treatment, or in whom the tendon has healed stretched out over time. A Cochrane systematic review comparing splinting and surgery concluded that there is not yet enough evidence to judge in which cases surgery is truly needed. So the decision is made by looking at each patient's degree of injury and life circumstances together. This patient chose surgery in view of these points. What is skin-tenodermodesis? The tendon at the end of the finger is very thin and flat, so if the tendon is stitched only to itself, its holding power is weak and it tears again easily. Skin-tenodermodesis is an operation that removes a section of the stretched tendon together with the skin above it to shorten its length, and encourages the tendon and skin to attach firmly to each other. It is simple and gives stable results, so it is used when splint treatment has failed or for old mallet fingers. ① Stretched tendon Cutting across the end joint reveals the stretched, scarred tendon. ② Remove the excess tendon The stretched part is cut out in an oval and the end joint is fixed straight with a wire (gray). ③ Tendon suture The tendon is stitched together, and the ends of the suture are secured outside the skin and removed at week 4. ④ Skin suture The excess skin is trimmed and sutured, and the stitches are removed at week 2. The wire is removed at week 6. Figure. A simplified redrawing of the steps of the modified skin-tenodermodesis introduced by Professor Joon Goo Lee's research team. After the sutures were completed. The blue thread is a suture that supports the tendon; it is secured outside the skin and removed at week 4. The end joint was fixed in a straight position with a wire (K-wire). The 6-week recovery 2 weeks after surgery The skin had healed and the skin sutures were removed. 4 weeks after surgery The sutures supporting the tendon and skin together were removed. 6 weeks after surgery After confirming that the tendon had healed enough, I removed the wire that held the joint. For about 2 more weeks afterward he wears a splint at night that keeps the end joint straight, and from week 8 he moves it without restriction. On the left is 6 weeks after surgery and on the right is before surgery. The end segment that had been drooping is now straight. The end segment of the little finger, which before surgery drooped and could not be straightened on its own, regained a straight shape without flexion deformity and the ability to extend after 6 weeks. In closing If the end of a finger suddenly droops and will not straighten, suspect mallet finger and check with an X-ray for a bone fragment. A tendinous mallet finger with only a torn tendon is mostly treated with a splint that holds the end joint straight for at least 6 weeks . The most important thing during this period is not to bend the end joint. When a splint is hard to use, has failed or the injury is old, skin-tenodermodesis is a simple and stable option. Do not dismiss it as “just slightly bent”; the earlier you are seen after the injury, the more likely a splint alone will be enough. This article is general medical information. The treatment method can differ with the timing and degree of injury, your job and your lifestyle, so please confirm through an examination. References Lee JK, Kang S, Park JW. Current concepts in traumatic mallet finger management . Arch Hand Microsurg . 2023;28(3):137–149. Handoll HHG, Vaghela MV. Interventions for treating mallet finger injuries . Cochrane Database Syst Rev . 2004;(3):CD004574.

t: Total knee arthroplasty for end-stage osteoarthritis with severe valgus (knock-knee) deformity: a case
s: A case of knee replacement in end-stage osteoarthritis with both knees severely bent into knock-knees: why valgus arthritis is difficult, outer contracture and inner ligament laxity, assessing ligament function with stress X-rays before surgery, lateral soft-tissue release, and the change in leg alignment and walking after surgery.
k: valgus knee knock knee total knee arthroplasty end-stage osteoarthritis ligament imbalance stress x-ray lateral release robotic
b: Knee Total knee arthroplasty for end-stage osteoarthritis with severe valgus (knock-knee) deformity: a case Hee Seung Nam, MD, Orthopedic Surgeon · June 8, 2026 The patient in this case came in with severe knock-knees (valgus deformity) and knee arthritis. Her left knee had hurt for a long time, and 15 years earlier she had undergone a left hip replacement at another hospital after an accident. Both knees bent markedly outward, the left more than the right. Leg alignment: severe knock-knee, especially on the left The full-length leg X-ray, taken from hip to ankle in one image, shows a severe valgus deformity, especially on the left (the left hip replacement was done 15 years ago). Arthritis with valgus deformity accounts for about 10 to 15% of knee arthritis. It is less common than bow-legged (varus) arthritis, but the bone and ligament deformity is more complex and surgery is known to be more difficult. Preoperative full-length leg X-ray. The yellow lines are the weight-bearing lines from the center of the hip to the center of the ankle. Knee X-rays: end-stage arthritis with the cartilage worn away Right knee (standing) Left knee (standing) Taken with the knees slightly bent Axial view of the kneecaps (patellae) In both knees the joint space had completely disappeared and bone rubbed on bone: end-stage osteoarthritis, Kellgren-Lawrence (KL) grade 4 . Bone loss in the outer part of the thigh bone (lateral condyle) and hardened bone beneath the cartilage (subchondral sclerosis) were also clearly seen. The biggest challenge: collapsed ligament balance The hardest part of knee replacement in severe valgus knees is soft-tissue imbalance . When the leg has bent outward for a long time, the outer structures (lateral collateral ligament, iliotibial band, popliteus and others) contract and shorten, while the medial collateral ligament on the inner side stretches and becomes lax. So simply cutting bone cannot make the surgery succeed. If the ligaments on the two sides are out of balance, the implant may not seat properly or the knee may stay unstable after surgery. To prevent this, stress X-rays , taken while pushing the knee inward and outward, are used before surgery to assess whether the inner ligament works and how far the joint opens. Stress X-ray (both knees) Stress X-ray with a block between the knees Stress X-ray of the right knee Stress X-ray of the left knee If this test shows the medial collateral ligament is not working, a constrained condylar knee (CCK) , which provides more stability than a standard implant, may be needed. Fortunately, in this patient the joint opened about equally when pushed inward and outward, suggesting the inner ligament still worked to some degree. Based on this, I planned knee replacement with a lateral soft-tissue release to loosen the shortened outer tissues, and operated on the left knee first and then the right, using a robot (MAKO). After surgery: a straightened leg Before surgery After surgery. The weight-bearing line passes through the middle of both knees. The postoperative full-length X-ray shows the weight-bearing line (mechanical axis) from hip to ankle falling within the normal range of ±3 degrees in both knees. Aligning this axis correctly in knee replacement spreads the load on the implant's plastic part (polyethylene) evenly, reducing wear, and is the most important factor in making the implant last. Postoperative front X-ray of both knees Right knee, side view Left knee, side view The magnified X-rays also show the thigh-bone and shin-bone components seated stably along the axis. How her walking changed Proper correction leads to better walking. Before surgery, she could not put full weight on her legs because the knees were unstable and painful, and she limped. After surgery, with the leg axis straightened, she walks far more comfortably. Left: walking before surgery. Right: after surgery. In closing Valgus (knock-knee) arthritis is less common than bow-legged arthritis, but the bone and ligament deformity is complex and needs more careful surgical planning. The outer side is shortened and the inner ligament stretched, so ligament function is assessed with stress X-rays before surgery. If the inner ligament still works, the outer tissues are released to restore balance; if not, a constrained implant is considered. Straightening the leg axis is the key to making the implant last and walking comfortably. This article is general medical information. The surgical approach can differ with the degree of deformity, ligament condition and individual circumstances, so please confirm through a medical consultation. References Ranawat AS, Ranawat CS, Elkus M, Rasquinha VJ, Rossi R, Babhulkar S. Total knee arthroplasty for severe valgus deformity . J Bone Joint Surg Am . 2005;87 Suppl 1(Pt 2):271–284. Ritter MA, Faris PM, Keating EM, Meding JB. Postoperative alignment of total knee replacement. Its effect on survival . Clin Orthop Relat Res . 1994;(299):153–156.

t: Treatment options for tibial shaft fractures
s: Seven cases of tibial shaft fractures from stairs, scooters and car crashes, used to explain how to choose between intramedullary nails, plates and other treatments.
k: shin tibia tibial shaft fracture intramedullary nail
b: Fracture & Bone Treatment options for tibial shaft fractures Hee Seung Nam, MD, Orthopedic Surgeon · April 20, 2026 · Treatment choices seen through seven cases A tibial shaft fracture is a fracture caused by high-energy injury, mostly from stairs, scooters or traffic accidents. If it is not treated properly, malunion can change the alignment and have a bad effect on the patient's life. For that reason, a tibial shaft fracture has to be treated properly at the right time. Let me go through seven patients I treated recently, case by case. Case 1. A teenage girl who was hurt on stairs She came in after her body weight pressed on the shinbone going down stairs and caused a fracture. Not only the tibia but the fibula was also fractured. In the image you can see a displaced fracture of the left tibia. Because she was an adolescent who had almost finished growing, I used an intramedullary nail, which can treat the fracture without directly touching the fracture site. At 6 weeks after surgery I confirmed that alignment had been restored, and at 3 months the fracture line was almost invisible. In patients like this, a nail is a good choice. X-ray before surgery X-ray after surgery Case 2. A teenage boy who fell off a scooter He fell while riding a scooter and broke both the tibial shaft and the fibula. I judged that without surgery the alignment would change and the outlook would be poor, so I operated. On the AP image the difference in alignment may not look large, but on the lateral view you can tell that correcting the alignment helped. The fibula can be expected to act as a strut, so I did not fix it separately. At 5 months after surgery union was well advanced, and at 8 months I confirmed union. The nail is planned to be removed at 1 year. X-ray before surgery X-ray after surgery Case 3. A tall adult man in a motorcycle accident A young man who had a tibial shaft fracture in a motorcycle accident. What was unusual was that this patient was over 190 cm tall, so his tibial shaft was longer than other patients'. When I measured the length to the fracture site it was 390 mm. By AO standards the maximum length of tibial nail available is 330 mm, or 345 mm with the end cap. A nail is a good choice, but there is a limit to the instruments, so I performed plate fixation. After reducing it as well as possible, I fixed it with screws above and below the fracture. A nail of more than 400 mm would have been a better choice, but this is a case treated with a plate because of the limits of the instruments. X-ray before surgery X-ray after surgery Case 4. A tibial fracture in a patient with after-effects of polio There can be controversy in treating a patient who has had polio. This patient was active and loved exercise, so I went ahead with surgery. Because of polio, the patellar tendon of the leg was poorly developed and the space below the patellar tendon (infrapatellar space) was small, so finding the entry point for the nail was very difficult. After surgery the fracture line is slightly visible but the alignment was well restored overall, and since the operation the patient exercises freely as he likes. X-ray before surgery X-ray after surgery Case 5. A refracture at the site of an old fracture A woman in her 50s. In her youth she was treated with an Ilizarov frame at another hospital for a tibial shaft fracture, and this was a case in which a fracture occurred again at the site that had healed in a hypertrophic union. This patient is very difficult to treat. An intramedullary nail has difficulty passing because the inner diameter at the narrowest part (the isthmus) is too small, and if done wrongly there is a risk that the bone will split. For a plate, no product matches the contour of the bone, so it would have to be bent by hand in the operating room, which is also not easy. So I referred this patient back to the hospital where the Ilizarov treatment had been done so that she could be treated there. X-ray at the time of the visit Case 6. A young woman who fell while skating It was a typical unstable fracture with a large triangular fragment detached from the middle-to-lower tibial shaft, and a fibular shaft fracture was also present. Such fractures often result from a high-energy force, so not only the reduction but also the degree of soft tissue injury and the possibility of compartment syndrome must be carefully assessed. I treated it with a tibial intramedullary nail, but could not insert it as it was. I made a small incision over the displaced part, reduced it and then used the nail. When I inserted the nail during surgery a varus deformity appeared, so I removed the nail, corrected the alignment, checked the alignment again and then inserted the nail to achieve the final alignment. At 6 weeks after surgery the fracture line was almost invisible. X-ray before surgery X-ray after surgery Case 7. A 40-year-old man whose leg was injured by rebar The most notable feature of this patient was that the tibial shaft was impacted into the fibular shaft. This finding was also clearly visible on MRI, and attempts at reduction in the emergency room did not work well because the tibia and fibula were impacted. I planned the surgery in two stages. First I reduced it and operated on the fibula, and the reduction went well so the alignment of the leg was nearly corrected. Ten days later I performed the second operation on the tibia. When the initial tibia and fibula fracture is severe, I stage the surgery in this order to prevent compartment syndrome of the leg and to put reduction first. X-ray before surgery X-ray after surgery Summary We looked at seven cases. Even fractures that look like the same site must be treated in completely different ways depending on the patient's age, the cause of injury (stairs, scooter, skating, traffic accident), anatomical characteristics (tall stature, polio and so on) and past surgery. The most common and best treatment in the textbook is not the right answer for every patient. The case in which a plate was chosen because the patient was so tall that existing nails were too short, and the case in which, because past surgery had deformed the bone, another safest alternative was sought for the patient instead of a risky operation, show this. A doctor's role in fracture treatment does not end with joining the broken bone. The heart of it is to design the most appropriate method by weighing each patient's situation and the limits of the instruments, and to restore correct alignment and help the patient return to daily life and the sports he or she loves. Tibial shaft fractures mostly result from high-energy injuries. Please take care when riding a scooter or motorcycle, or when doing an unfamiliar sport (for example, skating). If you are in an accident, please see a specialist without delay and receive treatment suited to you at the right time. If you have questions, please write to doctornhs@naver.com . This article is general information. Treatment can differ with the location and pattern of the fracture, your age and lifestyle, so please confirm through an examination. t: Bone pain every time you sit: weaver's bottom and ischial bursitis
s: Common in people who sit at work for long hours and nicknamed 'weaver's bottom', ischial bursitis: causes, symptoms, a real patient's MRI, how to tell it from a lumbar disc problem, and treatment from cushions to injections.
k: buttock sitting pain ischial bursitis weaver bottom
b: Hip & Pelvis Bone pain every time you sit: weaver's bottom and ischial bursitis Hee Seung Nam, MD, Orthopedic Surgeon · September 10, 2026 Just as the lump on the outer side of the little toe in tailors who worked sitting cross-legged is called “tailor's bunion,” there is a condition in the buttock too that got its name from an occupation. It is weaver's bottom . The exact diagnosis of this condition, common among weavers who sat all day weaving cloth on a hard wooden chair, is ischial bursitis . A weaver weaving cloth on a hard wooden chair. An illustration made with AI to aid understanding. The bone that touches the seat when sitting: the ischial tuberosity The prominent part at the bottom of the pelvic bone that touches the seat when you sit on a chair is called the ischial tuberosity . It is what people commonly call the “sitting bone.” Between this bone and the buttock muscle (gluteus maximus) is a small fluid-filled sac that reduces friction, the bursa . What is interesting is that this area looks different when standing and when sitting. When standing, the thick gluteus maximus covers the ischial tuberosity, but when you bend the hip and sit, the gluteus maximus slides upward and the ischial tuberosity meets the chair with only fat and the bursa in between. Contrary to what you might think, we sit on bone, not on buttock muscle. Standing The gluteus maximus covers the ischial tuberosity and acts as a cushion. Sitting The gluteus maximus slides upward, and body weight falls directly on the ischial tuberosity and bursa. Figure. A simplified drawing of the structures around the ischial tuberosity. If you sit on a hard surface for a long time, the bursa is pressed repeatedly and minor damage accumulates. Then fluid fills the bursa, the wall thickens and chronic inflammation develops. This is ischial bursitis. Korean radiology research also names prolonged sitting and occupations with repeated irritation of the bursa, like weaving, as causes. A real patient's MRI This is the MRI of a patient who came with pain in the left buttock, in the area of the sitting bone. The images show slices in turn, moving from the top of the pelvis downward. Axial MRI (T2 fat-suppressed images) moving from the top of the pelvis downward. At the level of the ischial tuberosity, a white, swollen bursa appears on the right of the screen, that is, the patient's left. There is no such lesion on the right (left of the screen). Unlike the right buttock, a well-defined, brightly glowing (high signal intensity) mass of fluid is seen around the left ischial tuberosity. It is an ischial bursa thickened by constant friction and filled with inflammatory fluid. Patients like this complain, from the moment they sit down on the chair in clinic, of pain and stiffness as if a hard lump were under the buttock. In a Korean study that analyzed the MRI of 17 cases of ischial bursitis, the bursa appeared bright on T2 images in all, and its size averaged about 4.7 × 3.8 cm. In many cases there was bleeding into the bursa, or the wall was irregularly thickened and septated. So it is sometimes mistaken for a tumor, but it can be diagnosed on MRI from its characteristic location and fluid-sac shape. Who is the modern-day weaver? Weavers at a loom are hard to find today, but this condition is still common. People who sit to work for long hours : office workers who sit in the same position in front of a monitor all day, and people who drive for long periods Cyclists : those who put their weight on a narrow, hard saddle People with reduced buttock muscle and padding : when the buttock muscle has wasted with age or too little exercise, or the cushion covering the bone has thinned after major weight loss. In the MRI study above, too, the patients were aged 50 to 82 (average 64). People with inflammatory disease : with an inflammatory condition such as rheumatoid arthritis, it tends not to heal and to last long. Why it is easily mistaken for a lumbar disc problem Close to the ischial bursa pass the sciatic nerve running down the leg and the nerve that supplies sensation to the skin at the back of the thigh. So when pain radiates down the back of the thigh it can feel similar to sciatica from a lumbar disc. Many people dismiss it as simple muscle pain and suffer for a long time. Condition Feature Ischial bursitis It hurts right below the sitting bone and is tender to the touch. It is worse when sitting on a hard chair and better when standing up. Lumbar disc herniation or spinal stenosis Back pain together with numbness spreading from the buttock down the leg, sometimes with reduced sensation or muscle weakness. Hamstring tendinopathy or partial tear A problem of the hamstring tendon attached to the ischial tuberosity. It hurts when sitting too, but more when running or reaching the legs out while bending forward, and it can occur together with bursitis. Soft tissue tumor If bleeding or septa develop inside the bursa it can look like a lump, so it is distinguished with MRI. On examination I press on the sitting bone to see whether the usual pain is reproduced, and if needed use ultrasound or MRI to see whether the bursa is filled with fluid. In a Korean study analyzing 64 patients with ischial bursitis, 92% had pain on pressing the ischial tuberosity. Treatment starts with reducing pressure The most important prevention and first treatment is to reduce the pressure on the ischial tuberosity. Most people get better with step 1 below. Step 1 · Reduce pressure and medication Use a soft cushion, or one hollowed out at the sitting bone area to spread the pressure. A donut cushion with a hole only in the middle was originally made for tailbone pain, so if the sitting bone rests directly on the ring when you sit, it is not suitable. If you have to sit for long, get up and change position every 30 to 60 minutes, and add anti-inflammatory painkillers or shock wave therapy. In the long run, strengthen the buttock muscles to build the “built-in cushion” that protects the bone. Step 2 · Injection If it does not improve, a steroid and local anesthetic are injected into the bursa, or the accumulated fluid is drained. Because a nerve runs close by, it is safer to inject at the exact spot under ultrasound. Step 3 · Surgery In the rare case that it keeps recurring despite treatment, surgery to remove the bursa is done. In the Korean study above, followed for more than a year, 79.7% improved with step 1 conservative treatment, 17.2% needed an injection, and 3.1% (2 patients) went on to surgery. Patients with inflammatory disease tended not to respond well to conservative treatment. In closing If there is pain, and tenderness to pressure, right below the buttock bone that touches the seat when you sit (the ischial tuberosity), suspect ischial bursitis . When you sit, the buttock muscle slides upward and the bone and bursa take the weight , so the habit of sitting on a hard chair for a long time is the biggest cause. It can resemble a lumbar disc problem or a hamstring tendon problem, so if needed confirm with ultrasound or MRI. Most people improve with cushions, changing posture and medication , and injection or surgery is not often needed. If a sharp pain under the buttock comes every time you sit on a hard chair, it may be the body's “weaver's warning.” This article is general medical information. b: Patient education › Rehab after surgery Rehab after ACL reconstruction and meniscus repair Hee Seung Nam, MD, Orthopedic Surgeon · November 1, 2026 This is the rehab schedule for people who have had anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction or meniscus repair. In both operations it takes time for the new ligament or the sutured meniscus to heal firmly, so the brace angle and the amount of weight on the leg are increased a little each week. Exercise often, as much as you can! Week-by-week at a glance If the table is wider than the screen, swipe sideways to see it. Feature Week 1 Days 0–7 Week 2 Days 7–14 Week 3 Days 14–21 Week 4 Days 21–28 Week 5 Days 28–35 Week 6 Days 35–42 Week 7 Days 42–49 Week 8 Days 49–56 Week 9 Days 56–63 Brace angle 0–30° 0–45° 0–60° 0–75° 0–90° 0–105° 0–120° 0–135° Brace removed Weight bearing Toe touch 25% of body weight 50% of body weight 75% of body weight Full weight bearing Crutches Two crutches One crutch No crutches How to read the table Brace angle This is the range in which the brace lets the knee bend. 0–30° means you can bend from fully straight up to 30 degrees, and it increases by 15 degrees each week. Toe touch The operated leg only lightly touches the floor with the toes to keep balance, and almost no weight is put on it. 25%, 50%, 75% of body weight The proportion of your body weight placed on the operated leg. It is easy to get the feel by placing the operated foot on a bathroom scale and pressing down. For example, if you weigh 60 kg, 25% is 15 kg. Crutches Use two crutches up to week 7 and one in week 8, and walk without crutches from week 9. Exercises by stage 1 Early stage 0–8 weeks after surgery Knee extension With a pillow under the ankle, place both hands on the knee and press down gently to straighten it. Leg raise Lying down, lift the operated leg straight, pull the toes toward you, and hold for 10 seconds. Bend and straighten Bend and straighten the knee within the brace angle, focusing on recovering the range of motion. Heel raise Seated on a chair, lift the heels. The goals of this stage are to straighten the knee fully and not to lose thigh muscle. 2 Middle stage 8–12 weeks after surgery Starting machine exercises Start a stationary bike, leg curl and squat machine with light weights. Single-leg stand On level ground, spread your arms and stand on the operated leg to hold your balance. Wall squat Squat with your back against the wall. Control the way down slowly, and come up quickly. This is the period for regaining strength and balance. If pain or swelling gets worse, lower the intensity. 3 Late stage After 12 weeks Strength machine exercises Do leg press, leg extension and leg curl at a weight you can manage, and increase the weight once every 2 weeks. Single-leg stand on a trampoline Build balance by standing on one leg on an unstable surface. Brisk walking Walk briskly on a treadmill. Jogging Possible from 6 months after surgery. The timing of return to sports is decided together through strength testing and an examination. Contact the hospital right away if: You have a fever of 38 °C or higher, or pus or discharge comes from the wound Your calf is swollen and painful to the touch, or you are short of breath with tightness in the chest Your knee suddenly swells a lot, or the angle you could move before suddenly cannot be reached Your leg feels numb or the sensation is dulled This schedule is the standard guidance I give to patients I have operated on. t: Femoral neck fracture and hip replacement surgery: a guide
s: A guide for patients with a broken hip neck (femoral neck) and their families: how the hip is built, why a small fall can break it, why surgery is done quickly, screws vs joint replacement, hemiarthroplasty vs total hip replacement, real before-and-after X-rays, and the course from admission to discharge.
b: Patient education › Surgery guide · Hip Femoral neck fracture and hip replacement surgery: a guide Hee Seung Nam, MD, Orthopedic Surgeon · November 4, 2026 This guide is for patients facing surgery for a broken hip neck (femoral neck) and their families. It explains why surgery is done quickly, what operation is done, and how recovery goes afterwards. 1. How the hip is built Ball and socket: the ball at the top of the thigh bone fits into a cup-shaped socket in the pelvis. The neck of the thigh bone: the column that holds up the ball. It is thin and breaks easily. Risk to the blood supply: when the neck breaks, the blood flow to the ball is easily cut off. Normal hip (dotted line: the neck that breaks easily), hemiarthroplasty (ball and stem replaced), total hip replacement (pelvic socket replaced as well). 2. Why a small fall can break it Osteoporosis: with age, the inside of the bone becomes porous and weak. Minor falls: even the impact of slipping at home can break it. 3. Why surgery should be done quickly Lying in bed for a long time causes dangerous problems like these. Having surgery quickly and getting up to move is the best prevention. Pneumonia: phlegm is hard to cough up, and the lungs become infected. Pressure sores: skin under pressure loses its blood supply and breaks down. Blood clots: a clot formed in a leg vein can break off and block vessels in the lungs, heart or brain. 4. Screws or a replacement? Patient and fracture Surgery Younger patient, slightly displaced bone Fixing your own bone: screws or similar implants hold your own bone firmly. Tried first when the bone is less displaced. Older patient, badly displaced bone (most cases) Joint replacement: the displaced bone has lost its blood supply, so the ball is replaced to avoid it dying (avascular necrosis). Practice standing can start the day after surgery. A case of fixation in a younger patient is shown in A Hip Neck Broken in Her 50s: Fixing It with an FNS Instead of a Joint Replacement . 5. Hemiarthroplasty vs total hip replacement Hemiarthroplasty (the standard treatment for fracture): only the broken ball side is replaced, and your own pelvic socket is kept. Total hip replacement: both the ball and the socket (pelvic side) are replaced. Mainly for people who already had severe arthritis. 6. Before and after surgery: real cases X-rays of three patients who had a hemiarthroplasty for a left femoral neck fracture. Case 1 before surgery: the neck of the left hip is broken and completely displaced. Case 1 after surgery: an implant placed by hemiarthroplasty. Case 2 before surgery: the neck of the left hip is broken and completely displaced. Case 2 after surgery: an implant placed by hemiarthroplasty. Case 3 before surgery: the neck of the left hip is broken and completely displaced. Case 3 after surgery: an implant placed by hemiarthroplasty. 7. From admission to discharge The day after surgery: start sitting in a wheelchair and practice standing with a walker. About 14 days after surgery: once the wound has healed, stitches are removed and discharge is planned. Positions to avoid after discharge: do not sit with your legs crossed or squat on the floor. The schedule can differ depending on the patient's condition. For life after discharge, see also After hip replacement: discharge and outpatient guide . 8. What to check after discharge Contact the hospital right away if: If the wound becomes warm or oozes fluid If the operated leg suddenly becomes shorter or turns so you cannot put weight on it (possible dislocation) To prevent a second fracture The most important things are preventing falls and treating osteoporosis. Keep up osteoporosis treatment, such as bone injections or pills, at your outpatient visits ( osteopenia column ). This guide is general information for people having surgery for a femoral neck fracture. Treatment and schedules can differ with each patient's condition, so please follow your surgeon's instructions first.

s: A guide for patients going home after hip replacement: suture removal and showering, positions that prevent dislocation for 3 months, walking rehabilitation, when you can drive, and symptoms that need a call to the hospital right away, with illustrations.

b: Patient education › Rehab after surgery · Hip After hip replacement: discharge and outpatient guide Hee Seung Nam, MD, Orthopedic Surgeon · November 2, 2026 This is guidance for people leaving the hospital after hip replacement. The key is to be careful about posture and steadily increase walking until the new joint settles firmly into the surrounding muscles and joint capsule, especially for 3 months after surgery . Before surgery. The cartilage of the hip joint on the right side of the image (the patient's left) is worn and the joint space is almost closed. After surgery. A cup on the pelvic side, and a metal stem and round head on the thighbone side, form the new joint. After discharge at a glance Discharge Come to the outpatient clinic regularly for X-rays and examinations. Take the medicine given at discharge until the next visit. Day 14 The stitches are removed. You can shower under running water from the next day . 1 month Activities that involve long immersion in water, like saunas and swimming pools, become possible. Once you can march in place without a walker, try walking without a walker together with a caregiver. 4–6 weeks If the right hip was operated on, you can begin to try driving slowly from this point. 3 months The period of dislocation precautions ends. Long drives are also recommended from this point. Medication and wound care You can take the medicine given at discharge until the date of your next outpatient visit . If side effects occur or are suspected, please call the main number of the hospital where you had surgery. Stitches are removed on day 14 after surgery, and you can shower under running water from the next day. Activities with long immersion in water, such as saunas, swimming pools and bathhouses, should be done, if possible, after 1 month following surgery. For 3 months after surgery: positions that prevent dislocation When the head of the artificial joint comes out of the cup, it is called a dislocation . Until 3 months after surgery, the tissues around the joint are still healing, so there is a risk it can come out in certain positions. The basic rule is to keep your legs as far apart as possible . Positions to avoid Squatting Sitting with legs crossed Sitting down on the floor in a W shape Do this instead Sit on a chair (with the hips higher than the knees) Put a pillow between your legs when turning over Spread your legs when lying down Change how you live at floor level. If you were used to living on the floor, it is best to change your habits to sit on a chair and sleep in a bed. Put a pillow between your legs when you roll over. So that your legs do not cross when you turn from lying on your back to your side, always change position with a pillow or similar object between your legs. Small tips for daily life Avoid chairs and sofas that are too low, and if the toilet is low, a raised toilet seat makes it easier. So as not to bend deeply at the waist when putting on socks or shoes, a long shoehorn or a sock aid is helpful. When getting into a car, sit on the seat first and then swing both legs in together. Depending on the surgical method, the positions to be especially careful about may differ a little, so if your doctor has given you separate instructions, follow those first. Walking is the best rehab The best rehab after surgery is to walk steadily and increase a little at a time . Put your weight on the healthy leg, and gradually increase the weight on the operated leg. Increase the amount of exercise little by little within what you can do. Increasing suddenly causes pain and swelling, so it is best not to overdo it. Keep increasing the amount you walk during the first month after surgery, and when you can march in place without a walker , try walking without a walker with the help of a caregiver. On stairs it is easier to step up with the healthy leg first and down with the operated leg first . Please avoid, as far as possible, sports that put heavy impact on the joint, such as hiking, marathons, basketball and soccer. Driving If the right hip was operated on, try driving slowly from 4–6 weeks after surgery, and it is best to drive for long periods only after 3 months , once you have recovered fully. If the left side was operated on, please discuss when to drive at your outpatient visit. Contact the hospital right away if: When the operated leg suddenly looks shorter or is turned outward or inward with severe pain and you cannot put weight on it (suspected dislocation) When you have a fever of 38 °C or higher, or the wound is red and swollen with discharge or pus Your calf is swollen and painful to the touch, or you are short of breath with tightness in the chest When the operated hip hurts after a fall This guidance is general information for people who have had hip replacement. It can differ with the surgical method and the patient's condition, so please give priority to the instructions of the doctor at the hospital where you had surgery.

b: Research Research and Publications Hee Seung Nam, MD, Orthopedic Surgeon · Updated November 2, 2026 I test the questions that arise in clinic through research and bring the results back into practice. The research is organized by field, done with the knee team at Seoul National University Bundang Hospital and the bone and soft tissue tumor team at the Korea Cancer Center Hospital. 23 articles Journal articles 6 articles First-author articles 5 articles Published in KSSTA (official journal of the European Society of Sports Traumatology, Knee Surgery and Arthroscopy) 4 articles Artificial intelligence studies Featured research Level of evidence 1 · Randomized controlled trial · First author If you explain “realistic expectations” before surgery, does satisfaction after joint replacement rise? 172 patients about to have joint replacement were randomly divided into two groups. One group received the usual education only; the other received additional education that explained the recovery course and realistic expectations in detail. One year after surgery, 83% were satisfied, compared with 65% in the group that received only the usual education. The difference was larger in people with a constitution especially sensitive to pain (central sensitization). I also did a follow-up randomized study (2025) tracking the same patients to two years. The difference in satisfaction at one year had disappeared at two years . The effect of less pain and stiffness appeared from 6 months, and the effect on pain lasted to one year. It means that explanation before surgery helps people get through the hardest first year of recovery. That is why I take time to explain before surgery. The first study was published in KSSTA (2023), the official journal of the European Society of Sports Traumatology, Knee Surgery and Arthroscopy (ESSKA), and the follow-up in the same journal (2025). See the 2023 paper → See the 2025 follow-up paper → Analysis of 863 patients · First author Do iron injections after joint replacement help? I compared 863 patients who had joint replacement, between those who received an intravenous iron injection afterward and those who did not. In the iron group, hemoglobin fell less and recovered better at 2 and 6 weeks after surgery, and among those who had both knees done in separate operations, the hospital stay was also shorter. However, there was no difference in transfusion rate, complications or final functional outcome . Only by knowing both the effect and the limits can I recommend it to the people who truly need it. Artificial intelligence · 3 first-author articles Reading the outcome in advance from a single image and preoperative information I built a deep learning model that predicts whole-leg alignment from an ordinary knee X-ray alone, and it showed accuracy similar to values measured directly on a full-leg film. I also developed a model that predicts satisfaction after joint replacement from preoperative information, and a model that picks out cases in bowed-leg correction that need a two-level osteotomy. I think of artificial intelligence not as a tool that replaces clinical care but as a tool that double-checks information easily missed in the same image. Bone and soft tissue tumors: 4 articles The rarer the tumor, the more important the record At the Korea Cancer Center Hospital I analyzed the treatment results of extraskeletal myxoid chondrosarcoma and myxoid liposarcoma, and the survival and complications of patients with a malignant bone tumor whose entire femur was replaced with a prosthesis. For tenosynovial giant cell tumor of the knee, I summarized how effective arthroscopic excision is depending on the extent of spread. b: Q&A Q&A: Questions and Answers Hee Seung Nam, MD, Orthopedic Surgeon I answer questions sent by visitors. I choose questions that many people share, remove personal details, and post the answers here. Tap a question to see the answer. Have a question? Send it through the form below. No name or contact details are needed. The question form will open soon. I answer general questions. I cannot diagnose or prescribe for individuals, or review your images. Not every question can be answered, and answers may take time. For emergencies or severe injuries, call 119 or go to the nearest emergency room. All 9 Knee 2 Hip 1 Foot & Ankle 2 Fractures & Bone Health 3 Lumps & Tumors 1 Q How many years does a joint replacement last? Knee A In a study pooling joint registry data from the UK, Australia and other countries, about 82% of total knee replacements and about 70% of partial knee replacements lasted 25 years without another operation. Managing your weight, avoiding high-impact activities such as running and jumping, and having regular check-ups help them last longer. Related: Total knee arthroplasty for end-stage osteoarthritis with severe valgus (knock-knee) deformity: a case · Getting to know robotic partial knee replacement 2026.11.09 Q When can I walk after hip replacement? Hip A Most people begin practicing standing with a walker the day after surgery. Walking distance is increased gradually with pain and condition, and for about three months after discharge you avoid positions that can cause dislocation, such as crossing your legs or squatting. The exact schedule depends on the operation and your condition. Related: After hip replacement: discharge and outpatient guide · Femoral neck fracture and hip replacement surgery: a guide 2026.11.09 Q My knee popped and is swollen. Is it a meniscus tear? Knee A It may be. Especially in middle age, pain that starts with a pop on the stairs or when squatting raises suspicion of a meniscus root tear. Left untreated, a root tear can speed up arthritis, so it is worth checking with an MRI. Not every meniscus tear needs surgery, though; treatment depends on the tear pattern and location, your age and your symptoms. Related: If you heard a 'pop' on the stairs: meniscus root tear · A 'pop' in the knee on a downhill walk: a radial meniscus tear and arthroscopic repair 2026.11.09 Q Do I have to remove the metal plate in my body? Fractures & Bone Health A In most cases, no. Removal is considered when the plate catches or hurts under the skin, when there is infection, or in growing children and young, active people. Removal surgery has its own risks, such as nerve injury or the bone breaking again, so the decision weighs discomfort against risk. Related: Do you have to remove the metal plate in your body? When is it removed? 2026.11.09 Q I can feel a lump. Could it be cancer? Lumps & Tumors A Most lumps in the body are benign. A lump larger than 5 cm, deep, growing quickly or painful needs a thorough work-up. A lump that tingles when tapped may be a nerve tumor, so do not squeeze or remove it yourself; have it checked. Related: A lump you can feel: lipoma or sarcoma? · A bulging lump at the base of the thumb turned out to be a schwannoma growing from a nerve 2026.11.09 Q How can I tell a calf strain from an Achilles tendon rupture? Foot & Ankle A When the Achilles tendon ruptures, it often feels as if someone kicked you just above the heel or you hear a pop, and you usually cannot stand on your toes. Because other muscles still allow some walking, it is easily mistaken for a strain, so see a doctor right away if you have these symptoms. If treatment is delayed, the tendon ends retract and repair can become difficult. Related: Like being kicked from behind: Achilles tendon rupture 2026.11.09 Q My child broke a collarbone. Does it need surgery? Fractures & Bone Health A Most heal well without surgery. A child's bone has a thick periosteum and a strong ability to remodel, so it recovers well even when somewhat displaced. The lump (callus) felt during healing is normal and mostly flattens as the child grows. Surgery is considered when bone has broken through the skin or nerve or blood vessel injury is suspected. Related: How should a child's clavicle fracture be treated? 2026.11.09 Q I was told I have osteopenia. Do I need medication? Fractures & Bone Health A Osteopenia is the stage before osteoporosis, and not everyone needs medication. Whether to treat is decided by assessing future fracture risk from age, previous fractures, family history and other factors. Strength exercise and walking, calcium and vitamin D, not smoking, limiting alcohol and preventing falls help everyone. Related: The first signal your bones send: osteopenia 2026.11.09 Q When should hallux valgus (bunion) be operated on? Foot & Ankle A Surgery is not done for the shape of the big toe alone. It is considered when pain continues despite conservative treatment such as wider shoes and orthoses, or when wearing shoes and walking become difficult. The operation depends on the degree of deformity and the condition of the joint. Related: Hallux valgus: when should you think about surgery? 2026.11.09 Answers are general medical information and do not replace an examination. Diagnosis and treatment depend on each person's condition, so please see a doctor if you have symptoms. Answer figures on joint replacement lifespan: Evans JT, et al. Lancet . 2019;393:655–663.
